title: Former Disney Channel star alleges she was sexually abused at 14 after being told to ‘bond’ with employee
summary: Raquel Lee Bolleau alleges an adult employee sexually abused her when she was 14 on a Disney Channel set after personnel encouraged her to "bond" with him.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
A former Disney Channel star made disturbing allegations about her time on set in a new lawsuit.
Raquel Lee Bolleau claimed an adult male employee sexually abused her when she was just 14 after Disney personnel allegedly encouraged her to "bond" with him.
The alleged abuse began during production of the 2001 Disney Channel movie "The Poof Point," after personnel directed her to spend time with the adult employee.
FORMER DISNEY STAR MAITLAND WARD SAYS YOUNG ACTORS WERE TREATED LIKE A 'PRODUCT' IN HOLLYWOOD FACTORY
According to the complaint obtained by Fox News Digital, the man supplied the 14-year-old with alcohol and repeatedly sexually assaulted her during filming.
After the alleged sexual assault, Bolleau recalled the employee telling her, "You're old enough. You can handle it."

Former Disney Channel star Raquel Lee Bolleau sued The Walt Disney Company, alleging an adult male Disney employee repeatedly sexually assaulted her when she was 14 while filming the 2001 movie "The Poof Point." (Michael Tran/AFP)

Bolleau claimed she returned to set smelling of alcohol, vomiting and visibly changed after the alleged assault, but Disney personnel failed to investigate how a 14-year-old got alcohol or seek medical care for her. Instead, the complaint claimed, an executive branded her "out of control," said the movie had gone "haywire" and told her representatives Disney was "extremely upset."

On another occasion, an on-set Disney executive producer allegedly repeatedly told Bolleau she "need[ed] Jesus" and told her mother, "your daughter has a demon inside her," according to the complaint.
Bolleau alleged Disney repeatedly separated her from her guardian despite California protections requiring a guardian of a performer under 16 remain within "sight or sound" of the child.

According to the complaint, her guardian could not watch Bolleau while she filmed or accompany her to wardrobe and makeup, and production personnel once told the guardian, "We do not even need you on set." Bolleau claimed those practices left her without adequate adult supervision and gave her alleged abuser unrestricted access to her.

Raquel Bolleau claimed Disney personnel directed her to "bond" with the employee, separated her from her guardian and later ignored signs of alleged abuse, including her arriving on set intoxicated and vomiting. (Ari Perilstein/Getty Images for Ramit Varma)
'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' STAR SAYS CHILD ACTORS GET 'DROPPED' AFTER HOLLYWOOD FAME FADES

Bolleau alleged the employee also sexually harassed and touched her in front of others on set. She claimed he regularly gave her unsolicited hugs, rubbed his genitals against her and whispered comments including "last night was so good" while cast members were still wearing microphones. Bolleau alleged sound technicians could hear many of the comments, but no one intervened or asked what the adult employee was saying to her.

"Instead of protecting and supporting its minor employee who was being repeatedly raped, sexually assaulted, sexually abused, and harassed, Disney covered up Mr. Doe’s abuse, and blamed Ms. Bolleau for the impact of Mr. Doe’s horrific misconduct," Bolleau's lawyers wrote.

"Disney’s egregious role in Mr. Doe’s abuse of Ms. Bolleau is part of a broader, institutional, and systemic pattern of institutional and individual failures at Disney that extends far beyond 'The Poof Point.'"

Bolleau claimed the alleged abuse continued after filming wrapped. According to the complaint, Disney booked Bolleau in first class while seating her guardian in economy on the flight back to California.

Bolleau alleged the employee told her to sit next to him and bring a blanket to cover them before sexually assaulting her during the flight and continuing until their row began to deboard at Los Angeles International Airport.

Raquel Bolleau, seen with husband Edouard Bolleau, alleged Disney executives blamed her for her deteriorating behavior and performance rather than investigate what was happening. (Rodin Eckenroth/Getty Images)

Bolleau sued The Walt Disney Company, specifically alleging Disney failed to protect her from sexual abuse when she was a 14-year-old actress. She claimed the company ignored warning signs, violated child-actor protections and failed to properly supervise her alleged abuser. She is seeking compensatory and punitive damages, along with attorneys’ fees, costs and interest.

"Over the last decade, countless child actors have come forward to bravely share their experiences of abuse by adults in entertainment," Bolleau's lawyers, Doug Wigdor and Jane Kim, told Fox News Digital in a statement.
"As former government prosecutors, our message to the entertainment industry is simple: This conduct is inexcusable, and those involved – directly or indirectly – must be held accountable."

Bolleau began acting as a child, with an early television appearance on "Malcolm & Eddie" before getting her breakout opportunity on Nickelodeon’s "The Amanda Show."

She appeared as a regular performer during the sketch comedy series’ first season alongside Amanda Bynes. She subsequently moved into Disney projects, playing Marie, the sister of Tahj Mowry’s Eddie, in "The Poof Point."

title: Country singer Lauren Alaina credits small-town Georgia roots for strong work ethic, faith
summary: Lauren Alaina reveals how growing up in Rossville, Georgia shaped her faith and work ethic ahead of her deeply personal fourth album, "Stages."
story: When speaking with Fox News Digital, Alaina said she comes "from a long line of hardworking people and believers" who taught her the importance of "working hard and having a strong faith."
Country singer Lauren Alaina is thankful for her small town roots and the lessons they taught her.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 31-year-old singer spoke about her upcoming album, "Stages," and shared why she credits growing up in Rossville, Georgia for her success and her work ethic.

"I come from a long line of hardworking people and believers and dreamers in their own way, whatever their path was," she said. "Mine obviously looked very different than the rest of my family because my working hard and my dreaming was leaving home and going to a new place, which people don't do a ton in Rossville, Georgia."

She explained that not only did she learn the importance of working hard from growing up in her small town, but also of "being kind, being grateful [and] being funny," saying she got her "sense of humor from back home for sure."

"I do think my work ethic definitely came from watching every one of my family. My mom worked really hard, my dad worked really hard, and my grandparents. They all had very different careers and different lives, but they just worked really hard and they kept their faith strong."
As an adult, she is now "thankful" to have grown up where she did and to have a strong faith and work ethic as some of the things were instilled in her throughout her upbringing.
Alaina is gearing up for the release of her fourth studio album, "Stages," which she calls "a deeply personal album," which covers three different phases of her life.

It is serious in parts and carefree and my mid 20s in parts and represents my hometown in parts as well. So I'm very proud of that."
The "Road Less Traveled" singer admits that each stage was hard for her to revisit, be it her parents' divorce, navigating heartbreak and losing her father unexpectedly.

title: Dolly Parton defied country music's expectations for women and built a career on her own terms: experts
summary: Dolly Parton broke barriers for women in country music by controlling her image, owning her work and refusing to shed her femininity for authority.
story: Fox News senior national correspondent William La Jeunesse goes through the legacy of country music legend Dolly Parton on 'The Story.'

From the get-go, Dolly Parton was a force to be reckoned with. She challenged social norms, broke barriers for women in country music and ultimately helped redefine what a female country star could be.

Throughout her life, Parton — who died Aug. 25 after a brief battle with cancer — helped "expand the narrative" of how women were perceived, not only in country music but beyond it, experts told Fox News Digital.

"Dolly followed some other pioneering women like Patsy Cline and Loretta Lynn who had already challenged expectations and proved that women’s experiences belonged in country music," Dr. Tracy King, a chartered clinical psychologist, writer and pop-culture commentator, told Fox News Digital.
DOLLY PARTON DIES AT THE AGE OF 80: A LOOK AT HER LIFE THROUGH PHOTOS
Dolly Parton paved the way for women in country music and beyond. (ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

"However, where they belonged was still within a narrow narrative of specific roles such as: the respectable woman, the suffering wife, the attractive female or the supporting partner to a more ‘powerful’ man."

"Dolly helped expand the narrative," King continued. "She could be the glamorous star, serious songwriter, ambitious decision-maker, owner of her work and a brand manager of her public identity all at the same time. She did not have to remove her femininity, accent or background to become powerful."
WHY DOLLY PARTON COULD BRING TOGETHER AMERICANS WHO AGREE ON ALMOST NOTHING

"This gave other women much more possibility," she added. "You could be emotionally open without being seen as weak, commercially ambitious without being masculine and visible without surrendering control of your story."
Dolly Parton died on Aug. 25. (AP Photo/Andres Kudacki, File)
Long before the rhinestones, platinum records and entertainment empire, Parton was one of 12 children raised in a one-room cabin in rural Tennessee, where money was scarce but music was a constant.
"I’ll always be a country musician because I’m a country girl," she told People in 1975. "My style is my soul and my feelings. I’ll tell the world in my songs what I wouldn’t have told my mother."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Parton would eventually turn the struggles and values of her childhood into the foundation of her songwriting.
Country singer Dolly Parton was one of 12 children. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
STEVE DOOCY: THE DOLLY PARTON I SAW WHEN THE CAMERAS STOPPED ROLLING

"Dolly refused to treat the things that made her different as problems that needed correcting," King said. "Her appearance became instantly recognizable, her voice very distinct and her background became central to the stories she told."

"She did not deny the poverty of her childhood, but she refused to accept that it made her inferior," King continued. "In ‘Coat of Many Colors,’ the homemade coat for which she was mocked also represented her mother’s love. Dolly acknowledged the shame and hurt, but she didn’t allow the cruelest interpretation of that experience to become the only one."
DOLLY PARTON’S SIX-DECADE LOVE STORY WITH CARL DEAN BEGAN AT A LAUNDROMAT

"This is what it means to reclaim your story," she added. "We cannot always prevent other people from judging us, but we can refuse to let their judgment become our identity. Her accent and background also helped create trust. People felt that she remembered where she came from and had not reinvented herself by rejecting her earlier life. She became successful without treating the person she had once been as someone who needed to disappear."
Parton was proud of her upbringing and used her values as a stepping stone into building her empire. (WireImage)
But Parton’s roots weren’t the only thing she refused to shed on her way to the top.
The Grammy Award winner leaned heavily into her trademark appearance — refusing to accept the idea that femininity and authority were mutually exclusive.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Dolly understood the assumptions people made about her appearance and used humor to demonstrate that she knew exactly what they were thinking," King said. "She was in on the joke, but she was never the joke."
Parton "consciously created her image" rather than allowing the industry to create it for her, King said.
DOLLY PARTON REFUSED TO PICK POLITICAL SIDES FOR DECADES: ‘I’M NOT IN POLITICS, I’M AN ENTERTAINER’

"The contrast between that image and her intelligence made other people’s prejudice visible," she said. "It exposed the judgers. Women are still frequently told that authority must look restrained, serious and almost masculine. Dolly rejected that. She did not change her appearance to prove she was intelligent; she made her intelligence impossible to deny and that femininity could run alongside and did not have to be denied."
Parton’s carefully constructed image didn’t prevent her from earning respect.
It became part of what made her success so significant.
Parton was known for her trademark appearance. (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Na)
TRUMP MOURNS DOLLY PARTON, ORDERS US FLAGS LOWERED NATIONWIDE AFTER COUNTRY MUSIC ICON DIES
Professor Susan McClary, a professor of music at Case Western Reserve University, said Parton entered the industry with "two strikes against her" — only to turn both into strengths.

"When Dolly Parton began her career, she had two strikes against her: she performed country music — a genre disdained by many listeners; and she presented herself in her attire and make-up as a cartoonish stereotype," McClary said. "Through perseverance, talent, self-deprecating sense of humor, and generosity, she managed to win over a vast fanbase while never compromising her values."
"Feminists who might have dismissed her appearance came to see her as a role model who insisted on creating and maintaining her own image," McClary said.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Parton passed away after a brief battle with cancer. (Shirlaine Forrest/WireImage)

But Parton’s determination to control her own identity extended far beyond her looks. Behind the larger-than-life image was a savvy songwriter and businesswoman who was equally determined to control her own work.

"Dolly built on the groundwork of Kitty Wells, Patsy Cline, Loretta Lynn and Tammy Wynette and expanded the range of what a female country performer could become," King said. "She opened the door to women being recognized as authors of their careers rather than being selected and managed by men. She wrote her own material, protected her publishing rights, left a successful partnership with a powerful male performer and developed businesses beyond the control of the traditional Nashville system."
"She showed younger artists that creative freedom depends not only on being heard, but on retaining ownership and decision-making power," she added.
Parton also demonstrated that female country artists did not have to remain confined to what society expected of them.
Parton paved the way for female country stars such as Reba McEntire, Shania Twain and more. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"A female country artist could enter pop music, film and television, establish a production company, build businesses and still remain connected to country music," King said. "We can see elements of that broader template in the careers of performers such as Reba McEntire, Shania Twain, Faith Hill, Trisha Yearwood, The Chicks, Carrie Underwood, Miranda Lambert, Taylor Swift and Kacey Musgraves."

"Her songwriting opened another door by showing that women’s inner lives could carry major commercial songs," King added. "Female characters could be jealous, angry, ambitious, sexually judged, economically exploited, ashamed, heartbroken or ready to leave. Later female performers had greater permission to write from their own point of view rather than to present a version of womanhood that was comfortable for a male audience."
Parton’s influence ultimately stretched far beyond music.
Parton was proud of her charitable work through the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images for American Greetings)

She built a business empire centered in her home state of Tennessee, with Dollywood becoming one of the state’s most recognizable attractions. Her charitable work through the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library left another lasting mark.

The Imagination Library, inspired by Parton’s father, who never learned to read or write, provides free books to children from birth to age 5. The program grew into an international literacy initiative, distributing millions of books to children around the world.
Following Parton’s death, tributes poured in from some of the women who followed the path she helped widen.

"Dolly, thank you for all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth," Reba McEntire wrote on Instagram. "Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge huge heart. There will never ever be another you. We will remember and cherish every memory and every note you ever played and sang."
"Thank you, Lord, for Dolly," she concluded. "She’s gonna have a blast in heaven singing all her favorite songs with all her family and friends who have gone on before her."
Shania Twain also shared an emotional tribute, calling Parton her "mentor."

"Dolly was pure light sent from heaven," Twain wrote on Instagram. "My mentor is gone. My songwriting teacher and hero of grace and humility. There is a hole in my heart but the joy of just the thought of her smile will continue to fill me with inspiration for as long as I live."
Parton left a "blueprint" for female country artists. (Getty Images)
Decades after she first entered an industry with narrow expectations for female performers, Parton left women in country music with far more room to define success on their own terms, said King.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Dolly left female performers with a much wider blueprint: write the story, own the work, control your own narratives and shake off the ones anyone else may have given you," King said.

title: Dolly Parton offered to try experimental drugs if ‘no hope’ for cancer battle to help others, sister says
summary: Dolly Parton offered to let doctors test experimental drugs on her during her cancer battle, hoping what they learned could someday save others.
story: Dolly Parton, the Grammy-winning singer, songwriter and philanthropist whose career spanned over six decades, has died at 80.
Dolly Parton stared down her own health crisis with one final act of generosity in mind.

Parton had quietly battled cancer in the months before her death on Aug. 25. The "Islands in the Stream" singer had informed fans she was struggling with her health, but never disclosed details. As she privately faced the devastating diagnosis, she was already thinking about how her fight could help others.

title: Navy veteran trades military uniform for Miss Georgia sash following heartbreaking loss
summary: Jade Kircus, a former naval officer and mother of three, is competing in the Miss USA pageant after experiencing a miscarriage.
story: Miss Georgia USA Jade Kircus shares how she went from serving as a naval officer to competing for Miss USA and why faith guided her unexpected journey.
After eight years of serving her country in a Navy uniform, Jade Kircus is trading it for a pageant sash.
At 36, the wife and mother of three is representing Georgia in her first-ever pageant: Miss USA. The competition takes place Aug. 27 in Miami.

"To be quite honest, I've actually never considered doing pageants," the Navy veteran told Fox News Digital. "It's not that I didn't think they were wonderful, and I really admired the women who did them. I just was always in a season where I wasn't able to do them, and I'm finally in a season where I can give a hundred percent."

Miss Georgia USA’s Jade Kircus is competing in the Miss USA competition taking place on Aug. 27, 2026, in Miami, Florida. (Courtesy of Miss USA)

"And when I found out that my state didn't have an actual pageant, I signed up for the open casting call after praying about it for a long time. So, since October, I've prayed about it. And the door opened. I joined the open casting call and was selected as Miss Georgia USA."
Kircus said it's never too late to chase a dream — or a crown.

Jade Kircus served two sea tours aboard USS Wasp (LHD-1), based in Norfolk, Virginia, and USS Chung-Hoon, based at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. "I never thought that at this point in my life I would be doing something like this," she said.

"But you can do hard things. You can do hard things at any age, at any stage. And I think each person has their own season where they're able to step out, and they're able to really show up in a way that they never thought they could. And so, whoever is listening, I want you to know that today you can make a choice to change. Today, you can make a choice to be confident and become the woman or the man that God has called you to be. It's never too late."
WATCH: MISS GEORGIA USA SHARES JOURNEY FROM NAVY UNIFORM TO PAGEANT SASH
In October, Kircus decided to take a chance on pageants. Later that month, she learned she was pregnant.
"I said, 'OK, Lord, that's a closed door,'" she recalled.

"It’s never too late to go after a dream the Lord puts on your heart — with confidence," Jade Kircus told Fox News Digital. "And I’m so grateful I get to encourage women in that!" (Courtesy of Miss USA)
Months later, Kircus experienced a heartbreaking loss. In January, she had a miscarriage nearly 16 weeks into her pregnancy.
Jade Kircus is a proud married mom of three. (Courtesy of Miss USA)

"We lost our baby girl," she said, fighting back tears. "I remember holding her in the hospital through several traumatic moments before that. And I remember looking at her and being like, 'Wow, this life is so beautiful.' And it was in my most difficult moment that the Lord really showed up and showed me who He was. And although it was challenging, I clung to my faith."
Kircus said her faith helped her through the loss, giving her "peace" and strength to keep moving forward for her family.

Jade Kircus left the Navy in March 2020 after eight years of service and later worked as a government contractor at U.S. Special Operations Command as a deputy operations lead for several years. (Courtesy of Miss USA)

"In my hardest moment, I looked at that and was like, 'God, you're still faithful. You're still good. You still care about me deeply, and my baby girl is with you. I get to meet her one day because you're good.'"
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Jade Kircus suffered a devastating miscarriage before competing in Miss USA. (Courtesy of Miss USA)
Kircus said she spent January grieving. By February, she was ready to take a leap of faith and give herself something new to work toward.

"In February, God put Miss USA back in my heart," she said. "I'm like, 'OK, God, I thought it was a closed door, but it is an open door. And so, I'm not going to sit in the pain and the hard parts of what I just experienced. I'm going to move forward and know that you have a plan.'"
Jade Kircus told Fox News Digital her unwavering faith anchored her through a painful tragedy. (Courtesy of Miss USA)
"I miss my baby girl, and I wish I was holding her right now," she said. "I know that I'm here for a purpose, whatever that is, whatever that looks like."
Jade Kircus told Fox News Digital she became a "full-time stay-at-home momma by choice" in 2024. (Miss USA)
Pageantry is far different from Navy service, but Kircus said her training prepared her for the challenge.

"The Navy really taught me determination," she said. "It taught me resilience. It taught me how to lead with purpose, no matter the circumstances. Being a mother has also taught me those things, but it taught me so much about people, taught me how to love people even better, taught me how to raise the next generation, how to meet them where they're at, let them know they're valued, they have worth, they're loved."
Jade Kircus said becoming Miss USA would give her another opportunity to serve her country in a new way. (Courtesy of Miss USA)

"The Miss USA organization has taught me so much," she said. "Not only about just being able to step out and be bold wherever you're at, but also how to relate to people, how to truly be the best version of myself and not only lead people, but work with them to make a better community, a better world."

Jade Kircus is competing in her first pageant. (Instagram.com/all.things.jade/)

Kircus is a first-generation American whose parents are from Scotland and England. She served two sea tours before completing a shore tour at U.S. Central Command in Tampa. After leaving the Navy in 2020 and working for several years as a government contractor, Kircus chose to become a stay-at-home mother in 2024.
The Miss USA pageant dates to 1952, when Catalina Swimwear launched the competition after withdrawing its sponsorship of Miss America.
Miss USA was founded in 1952. (Bettmann Archive)
For Kircus, competing for the crown is another opportunity to serve.

"Representing the USA is one of the most incredible honors of my life," she said. "Not only have I experienced that as a naval officer, but I've experienced it as a daughter, as somebody who has parents who are not originally from this country. My heart has always been to serve, and representing the USA on an international scale really would be such an honor. And I do believe we can make an impact."
The Miss USA 2024 delegates pose onstage during the 73rd annual Miss USA Pageant at Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, on Aug. 4, 2024. (Getty Images)

"My goal is to let people know they can walk in confidence in whatever God has called them to do, because they have something to bring to the table," she said. "It's never too late to show up for your country. And that's the woman I want to be."

title: Gigi Hadid says her relationship with Bradley Cooper provides something she hasn't experienced before
summary: Gigi Hadid told Vogue France that deep honesty sets her Bradley Cooper romance apart, as marriage speculation swirls after their Paris ring sighting.
story: Supermodel Bella Hadid made a bold fashion statement as she arrived at the New York premiere of FX’s ‘The Beauty’ at the Museum of Modern Art.
Gigi Hadid is getting candid about what makes her romance with Bradley Cooper unlike the relationships that came before him.
In a new interview with Vogue France, the 31-year-old supermodel offered a rare glimpse inside her notoriously private relationship with the Oscar-nominated actor.
"What is beautiful about my current relationship, and so different from what I have experienced, is an ability to be deeply honest," Hadid told the outlet. "To say what you think, when you think it."
GOLDIE HAWN CREDITS ‘FREEDOM’ FOR KEEPING 43-YEAR RELATIONSHIP WITH KURT RUSSELL STRONG
Gigi Hadid started dating Bradley Cooper in October 2023. (TheStewartofNY/ GC Images)
When the interviewer noted that kind of honesty isn't always easy, Hadid didn't hesitate.
"I know. But if that's impossible, it probably means he's not the right person," she said.
Hadid's candid comments come weeks after she and Cooper, 51, fueled marriage speculation when they were photographed in Paris wearing matching bands on their left ring fingers.

Page Six reported earlier this month that the rings were Boucheron wedding bands, though neither Hadid nor Cooper publicly confirmed that they had tied the knot. Days later, Us Weekly reported, according to a source, that the jewelry was instead a pair of "promise rings" and that the couple was not married.
The pair, who have been romantically linked since late 2023, have largely kept their relationship away from the spotlight.
Hadid told Vogue in 2025 that the couple's decision to remain private wasn't necessarily strategic.
"It's just not part of our relationship to share for whatever reason," she said at the time, describing their relationship as "very romantic and happy."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Bradley Cooper and Gigi Hadid are seen in NoHo in New York City on Nov. 11, 2024. (Aeon/GC Images/Getty Images)
That privacy began to shift in May 2025, when Hadid made the romance Instagram official while celebrating her 30th birthday.
The model shared a series of photos from her birthday party, including one of her and Cooper kissing in front of a multi-tiered cake.
"I feel so lucky to be 30!" Hadid wrote at the time. "I feel so lucky for every high and low, for all the lessons and gifts both have brought me."
She added that she felt "so lucky to be a mom, friend, partner, sister, daughter, colleague to some of the most unbelievable humans."
Now, more than a year later, Hadid appears to be settling into a quieter chapter.
Asked by Vogue France how she was feeling, Hadid said friends have noticed a change.
"Right now my friends are saying to me: ‘Gigi, what's going on? Looks like you're 19 again,’" she said. "I just think I'm... serene."
OLIVIA WILDE BREAKS SILENCE ON HARRY STYLES FANS AND THEIR BRUTAL REACTION TO THEIR 10-YEAR AGE GAP ROMANCE
Bradley Cooper and Gigi Hadid attend Hadid's 30th birthday at Le Chalet in Midtown on April 25, 2025, in New York City. (Aeon/GC Images/Getty Images)
Part of that serenity appears to come from the life she has built away from the fashion industry's constant spotlight.
Hadid told the outlet that spending time in the countryside with her daughter, partner, friends and animals helps ground her before she returns to work.

"Living in the countryside surrounded by animals, with my daughter, my partner, my friends, is part of what recharges my batteries," she said. "It allows me to appreciate the richness of fashion when I come back to it."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Hadid shares daughter Khai with ex-boyfriend Zayn Malik, while Cooper shares daughter Lea with former partner Irina Shayk.
The model also said she and Cooper talk about their careers even if they don't always fully understand the demands of the other's profession.
"We don't necessarily understand all the challenges of each other's job, but the main thing is to have someone who supports you – and helps you keep your feet on the ground," Hadid told Vogue France.
When asked whether a strong relationship requires work from both people, Hadid offered another perspective.
Gigi Hadid and Bradley Cooper depart Madison Square Garden after the wedding of Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce in July. (Reuters/Bing Guan)
"I would say it's a trip for two," she said.
Her latest comments echo what she previously said about finding a partner who already understands what he wants from life.

"Knowing what you want and deserve in a relationship is essential, and then to find someone that is in a place in their life where they know what they want and deserve…and you both do work separately to come together and be the best partner that you can be," Hadid previously told Vogue.
"I just feel really lucky. Yeah, lucky's the word."
The couple's romance has also given Hadid a new way of experiencing one of the cities most closely associated with her career.
For years, she said Paris primarily meant work.
"I landed there, drove to the hotel where twenty photographers were waiting for me, impossible to walk, then in a car to a windowless studio," Hadid told Vogue France.
That changed through Cooper, whom she described as someone who loves France and speaks French.
HEIDI KLUM SHUNS HOLLYWOOD'S WEIGHT-LOSS OBSESSION AFTER HUSBAND TOM KAULITZ TOLD HER TO 'EAT MORE'
Bradley Cooper and Gigi Hadid are seen in the West Village on June 13, 2025, in New York City. (Aeon/GC Images/Getty Images)
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
"Except that, recently, thanks to my boyfriend who loves France and speaks French, I discovered a completely different Paris that I adore," she said.
Asked whether she could envision living there, Hadid didn't rule it out.
"So at some point, why not move there, yes..." she said.
Hadid's growing sense of peace also extends to how she views fame and the image of her life presented to millions of followers online.
"99% of my daily life is not online," she told Vogue France. "What I'm posting is my way of celebrating the wonderful things in life. But Instagram remains 1% of my life."
The model has lived much of her adult life in the public eye, becoming one of the industry's most recognizable faces while still in her teens.
She told Vogue France that the visibility she once dreamed about eventually became overwhelming.
"It was around the age of 19 that this visibility began," Hadid said. "At first, it's true that this is what you dream of. And, little by little, the noose tightens. You lose control."
"And it becomes overwhelming, because you end up only living through the eyes of others," she continued.
These days, Hadid said she has found a better balance between fame and her private life.
"Today, I have found a balance between my life as a mom in Pennsylvania and my public life," she said.

title: Dolly Parton’s six-decade love story with Carl Dean began at a laundromat
summary: Dolly Parton and Carl Dean's private love story began at a Nashville laundromat in 1964 and endured nearly 60 years away from the spotlight.
story: Kathie Lee Gifford shares personal memories from her close friendship with Dolly Parton on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’
Dolly Parton lived much of her life in the spotlight, but her greatest love story unfolded almost entirely away from it.

The country music legend, who died on Tuesday at the age of 80 after a "brief battle with cancer," was married for almost 60 years to her late husband Carl Dean. Parton's death comes less than 18 months after she lost Dean, who died in March 2025 at age 82.
While announcing her passing, her nephew Bryan Seaver shared their family's belief that she had been reunited with the man she called the "star of my life story."
TRUMP MOURNS DOLLY PARTON, ORDERS US FLAGS LOWERED NATIONWIDE AFTER COUNTRY MUSIC ICON DIES
"Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by Carl, her parents and countless others who have watched her and longed to meet her in the heavens," Seaver said.
Dolly Parton's love story with her husband Carl Dean began at a laundromat and lasted more than 60 years. (Getty Images/Getty Images for ACM; Dolly Parton Instagram)
Despite being married to the internationally famous singer, Dean was a very private man who steered clear of the limelight and was rarely seen in public.
The couple's romance began with a chance meeting on Parton's first day in Nashville in 1964. At the time, Parton was 18 and Dean was 21.

Parton, who hailed from rural East Tennessee, previously shared she had been so eager to leave home that she arrived in Nashville with dirty clothes and went to the Wishy Washy Laundromat. While her clothes were in the wash, she bought a cold drink and walked around looking at her new city.

Dean drove past in a Chevrolet and warned her that she was going to get sunburned. Parton, who said she greeted everyone because she was "straight from the country," answered him. He soon circled back and joined her at the laundromat.

"I was surprised and delighted that while he talked to me, he looked at my face, a rare thing for me," Parton recalled in a 2016 post on her official website. "He seemed to be genuinely interested in finding out who I was and what I was about."
Parton died on Tuesday, 17 months after Dean passed away. (AP Photo/Andres Kudacki, File)
During his lifetime, Dean rarely gave interviews. However, in 2016, he spoke lovingly of Parton while the couple were celebrating their 50th wedding anniversary.

"My first thought was, 'I'm going to marry that girl,'" Dean told Entertainment Tonight about meeting Parton for the first time. "My second thought was, 'Lord, she’s good-looking.' And that was the day my life began. I wouldn't trade the last 50 years for nothing on this Earth."

Two years after their first meeting, Parton and Dean married in a private ceremony in Ringgold, Georgia, on May 30, 1966. Parton’s record label had reportedly urged her to postpone the wedding for a year while launching her career, but the couple chose to marry quietly across the state line to avoid coverage in the Nashville press. Parton's mother, Avie Lee, was the only wedding guest.
"It was just my mother and Carl and me," Parton told CMT in 2016. "We went across the state line to Ringgold, Georgia. My mother made me a little white dress and a little bouquet and a little Bible."

Parton said she rejected the idea of a courthouse ceremony because she feared she would not "feel married." The couple instead found a small Baptist church, where Pastor Don Duvall married them before they posed for photographs on its steps. According to Parton’s official website, the pastor’s wife also attended.
Parton and Dean married during a private ceremony in Ringgold, Georgia in 1966. (DollyParton.com)

While Parton pursued her dream of country music stardom, Dean remained firmly outside the entertainment industry. He owned an asphalt-paving business in Nashville and preferred a quiet life on their farm away from the limelight, though Parton said he always supported her ambitions.

Early in their marriage, Parton persuaded Dean to accompany her to the BMI Awards, where she won her first songwriting award for 1966's "Put It Off Until Tomorrow," which was named song of the year. During a December 2024 appearance on Bunnie Xo’s "Dumb Blonde" podcast, Parton recalled renting Dean a tuxedo and begging him to attend.
"And, oh, he was so uncomfortable the whole night," Parton said.
DOLLY PARTON’S ONGOING HEALTH BATTLE FORCES COUNTRY LEGEND TO MISS MAJOR DOLLYWOOD EVENT
Parton remembered that Dean "started pulling off stuff" immediately after they returned home.

"He said, ‘Look, now I want you to do everything you want to do, and I wish you the best, but don't ever ask me to go to another one of these damn things because I ain't going.’ And he never did," she said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"So we just kind of have that respect, and I respected that because I didn't know he was gonna be that uneasy, but he doesn't even like to go out to, you know, to big dinners or anything like that," she added.
Over time, Dean's absence became so conspicuous that there was speculation that he didn't exist, and she had made him up to ward off admirers.
During a 2020 interview with Entertainment Tonight, Parton weighed in on the longtime rumors.
Dean shunned the spotlight throughout their marriage. (Dolly Parton Instagram)

"A lot of people have thought that through the years, because he does not want to be in the spotlight at all," she shared. "It's just not who he is. He's like, a quiet, reserved person and he figured if he ever got out there in that, he'd never get a minute’s peace and he's right about that."

"I've always respected and appreciated that in him and I've always tried to keep him out of the limelight as much as I can," Parton continued. "He said, 'I didn't choose this world, I chose you, and you chose that world. But we can keep our lives separate and together.' And we do and we have."

While Parton's career required constant travel, she previously said that Dean preferred staying at their Tennessee home and taking care of their ranch. While speaking with ET, Parton shared that the time spent apart strengthened their relationship.

"Our joke about the fact, when people ask me why it's lasted this long, I say, ‘Because I stay gone,’" she told ET. "And there's a lot of truth in that — the fact that we're not in each other's faces all the time.
"But we do have a great respect and admiration for each other. We both have a great sense of humor. So, we have a lot of fun," she added.
During a 2015 interview with People magazine, Parton shed some light on their favorite shared activities and their low-key home life.
DOLLY PARTON CANCELS LAS VEGAS RESIDENCY AS HEALTH ISSUES FORCE HER TO STEP BACK FROM STAGE PERFORMANCES

"We like to get out in our little RV and just be simple," she said. "I love to read, I love to cook, I love to be with my husband. I put on my little comfy clothes – I call them my baby clothes – and we just relax."
Dean only accompanied Parton to one industry event during their marriage. (David Redfern/Redferns)

"He loves to go on vacation or on little trips, but he doesn’t want to be gone a long time," Parton continued. "He wants to be mostly around the house. He knows I’m just the opposite. I can’t go enough places. I can’t do enough things. He loves that. He’s independent."
"But when we’re together, we have enough things in common that it works," she added. "We love the simple life. We can be calm and just have a good time."

Though Dean stayed out of the spotlight, his influence could be heard throughout Parton’s music. The country star previously said that a flirtatious red-haired bank teller’s interest in her husband helped inspire the story behind her 1973 hit "Jolene," while an early disagreement about Parton’s romantic past led her to write 1968's "Just Because I’m a Woman." She later said she thought of Dean while writing her 2012 song "From Here to the Moon and Back."

Dean’s love of rock music, particularly Led Zeppelin, also helped inspire Parton’s 2023 album "Rockstar." Shortly after his death, she paid tribute to him with "If You Hadn’t Been There," a song crediting him with supporting her and encouraging her dreams.
Parton called Dean the "star of my life story." (Terry Wyatt/WireImage)

Parton and Dean never had children, though she said they had imagined becoming parents early in their marriage and even chosen names. In 2017, Parton told The Guardian that they would have named a daughter Carla.

The "9 to 5" star previously said that she later came to believe not having kids allowed her to pursue her career and devote herself to other children, including her nieces and nephews and goddaughter Miley Cyrus, as well as those reached through her early-childhood literacy program Imagination Library.

"I didn’t have children because I believed that God didn’t mean for me to have kids, so everybody’s kids could be mine, so I could do things like Imagination Library, because if I hadn’t had the freedom to work, I wouldn’t have done all the things I’ve done," she said while appearing on 2020 episode of Apple TV+’s "The Oprah Conversation." "I wouldn’t be in a position to do all of the things I’m doing now."

In May 2016, Parton and Dean renewed their vows in a private Nashville ceremony on their 50th anniversary.

"We’re going to get married again!" Parton told People magazine at the time. "I’ll have a beautiful wedding dress, ’cause I didn’t have a big, long wedding dress when we got married, and we've got a suit for him, so we’re going to dress up and take a bunch of pictures."

Parton later celebrated their vow renewal ceremony in a June 2016 statement. "If I had it to do all over, I’d do it all over again, and we did," she said. "I’m dragging him kicking and screaming into the next 50 years."
On March 3, 2025, Parton announced Dean's death on social media, writing, "Carl and I spent many wonderful years together."
"Words can't do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years," she added. Thank you for your prayers and sympathy."
Days later, Parton released "If You Hadn't Been There" in honor of her husband and the cover art for the song featured a vintage photo of the couple.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I fell in love with Carl Dean when I was 18 years old," she wrote on Instagram at the time. "We have spent 60 precious and meaningful years together. Like all great love stories, they never end. They live on in memory and song. He will always be the star of my life story, and I dedicate this song to him."
Though no cause of death was disclosed, Parton later said her husband had "suffered a lot" during his final years.
During a June 2025 interview with The Associated Press, Parton opened up about how her belief in God has helped her navigate the grief she has endured in the wake of Dean's death.
"I am a person of faith, and I truly believe that I’m going to see him again someday," Parton said.
Parton said that she believes Dean is "waiting for me on the other side." (Dolly Parton Instagram )

In the months after Dean’s death, Parton revealed that she had neglected her own health while caring for her husband during his prolonged illness. She later battled a kidney stone infection and other health complications that forced her to postpone concerts and miss public appearances. However, Parton continued working and remained optimistic about her recovery until shortly before her death.

During a March 2026 appearance at Dollywood, Parton laughed off rumors that she was dating or had remarried, according to the Knoxville News Sentinel.

"I don't think I'll ever be married but once," she said. "I think Carl Dean’s waiting for me on the other side."

title: Busy Philipps diagnosed with rare brain tumor after undergoing body scan her doctor told her she didn't 'need'
summary: Busy Phillips revealed her grade 2 oligodendroglioma diagnosis came after a Prenuvo scan her primary care doctor initially said she didn't need.
story: Samantha Harris tells Fox News Digital people need to be their own "best health advocate." The TV personality was first diagnosed with breast cancer in 2014, then again in 2024.
Busy Philipps is sharing how she was diagnosed with a rare brain tumor.

During a recent interview with People magazine, the 47-year-old "Cougar Town" actress shared the terrifying moment her doctor told her she had a brain tumor, the day after her "Dawson's Creek" co-star, James Van Der Beek, died after a battle with colorectal cancer.
"Dr. Devinsky says to me, 'I'm just going to say this to you the way I would want someone to say it to me,'" she recalled.
'BACHELORETTE' STAR REVEALS BRAIN TUMOR DIAGNOSIS AFTER ROUTINE HEALTH SCAN

"And that was when the wind like sort of knocked out of me, and I had to sit down. He was like, 'I need you to breathe. I can hear that you're not breathing.' And I was like, 'Just tell me what's happening.' And he's like, 'This isn't any of those other things that they said it could be. This is a real tumor, and it's inside your brain, and Busy, it's got to come out. We got to take it out.'"
She was then connected with Dr. John Golfinos of NYU Langone and scheduled the five-hour surgery for March 2, during which surgeons removed a 2.6-centimeter mass from her brain.
Philipps shared she was diagnosed with a rare brain tumor in February. (Gilbert Flores/WWD via Getty Images)

The mass was then biopsied and revealed to be a grade 2 oligodendroglioma, a rare tumor that Dr. Alexandra Miller, Philipps’s neuro-oncologist at NYU Langone told People, affects 1,100 to 1,300 people a year in the U.S. She added that "it is considered malignant, but it has the best prognosis of all of the malignant gliomas."
"It’s sort of defined as a cancerous tumor based on the ability of the tumor to regrow over time, rather than it looking very malignant under the microscope," Miller said.

The diagnosis came after Philipps told her cousin’s husband, a doctor in Los Angeles, that she was interested in getting a Prenuvo scan but that her primary care doctor had told her in 2025, "You're super healthy. We've done all this other blood work. We've done, like, all kinds of tests. You're super healthy. There's no need for you to get one."

"'Oh, I love them,'" he told Philipps about the scan. "And I was like, 'OK, cause my doctor just a few months ago said that I shouldn't get one.' He's like, 'Oh, like respectfully, don't know your doctor, but disagree. I think knowledge is power.'
"And what he said really resonated with me. And I was like, 'That was kind of what I was feeling, too. I think I want to get one.' He's like, 'Well, I'd be happy to help you set that up.'"
Philipps' primary care doctor originally told her she didn't need a Prenuvo scan that detected her tumor. (John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images)
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

After getting the scan, the "Freaks and Geeks" star went to an audition and later that night got a call from her cousin's husband, who let her know there was a lesion on her brain and that she should get an MRI.
Dr. Devinsky later told her the MRI showed a tumor that needed to be removed.

Philipps’ neurosurgeon, Dr. John Golfinos, told People that the early detection of the tumor ultimately made the surgery much easier, adding that had the tumor been found later, it "would have been two or three times the size."
Over a month after recovery, Philipps was back on the operating table after her dermatologist flagged that her incision site looked concerning.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Philipps filmed the upcoming legal drama, "Cupertino," in between dealing with her health scares. (Unique Nicole/Getty Images)
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
She had contracted staphylococcus, which required another surgery to cure, leaving Philipps feeling "really upset" and "like I was back at square one."
Despite her health scares, Philipps still managed to film her upcoming legal drama, "Cupertino," in which she plays the ex-wife of an AI billionaire who becomes the financier of a new law firm.
Philipps does not need chemotherapy or radiation but will get regular scans to monitor any potential reoccurrence. Through this experience, the actress learned to trust her instincts.
"We are frequently told by doctors that there is nothing to worry about [when] you kind of know that there’s something to worry about," she said.
"There’s nothing to be afraid of in having information. It’s only empowering."

title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle arrive in UK with kids, marking dramatic return 6 years after royal exit
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle arrived at Birmingham Airport with Archie and Lilibet, but no visible police presence was reported at the scene.
story: Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair royal correspondent and co-host of "The Royals Uncensored," says Prince George passed Eton's admissions process like other applicants before accepting his place at the prestigious school.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are back in Britain — six years after leaving royal life behind for California.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex arrived at Birmingham International Airport around noon Wednesday with Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5. Their private flight from Van Nuys, California, landed shortly before noon, according to The Associated Press.
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK MOVE PUTS FRESH SPOTLIGHT ON THEIR EXPLOSIVE CLAIMS AGAINST ROYAL FAMILY
Meghan Markle and Prince Harry pictured at the Royal Children’s Hospital in Australia earlier this year. (Jonathan Brady-Pool/Getty Images)
There was no visible police presence as Prince Harry and his family left Birmingham Airport, according to The Telegraph, with the couple instead relying on their own security team.
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s team for comment.
PRINCE HARRY AND MEGHAN MARKLE WON’T ‘HIJACK’ PRINCE GEORGE’S HISTORIC ETON DEBUT, ROYAL EXPERT SAYS
The return comes just days after Harry and Meghan announced plans for an "extended" stay in Britain.

Archie and Lilibet are enrolled in British schools and are expected to begin classes in September. Harry and Meghan plan to live at a private, non-royal residence outside London, although they have not disclosed the location. They will also keep their California home.

title: Tim Curry, 'The Rocky Horror Picture Show' actor, dead at 80
summary: Tim Curry, the British actor who portrayed Dr. Frank-N-Furter in "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," died Tuesday at 80 after years of stroke recovery.
story: Fox News’ William La Jeunesse looks back at the life and career of actor Tim Curry, known for memorable roles in ‘The Rocky Horror Picture Show,’ ‘Clue,’ ‘It’ and more.
Tim Curry, best known for playing Dr. Frank-N-Furter in "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," has died. He was 80.

Curry's death was confirmed by his publisher, Jimmy Franco, senior director of publicity at Grand Central Publishing. "Yes, it is true and very sad indeed." Franco added that he did not have a statement to share at this time.

The LAPD confirmed to Fox News Digital that officers responded at approximately 11:20 p.m. Tuesday for a death investigation involving a male described as being in his 80s at home. No foul play is suspected.

Curry became a pop-culture icon after starring as Frank-N-Furter in the 1975 film "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," having originated the role in the original 1973 London stage production before taking it to Broadway and the big screen.
DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80

Tim Curry is remembered for his unforgettable roles on stage and screen, including his iconic turn as Dr. Frank-N-Furter in "The Rocky Horror Picture Show." (Walt Disney Television Photo Archives/Walt Disney Television via Getty Images)
The cult classic, which also starred Susan Sarandon, Barry Bostwick and Meat Loaf, became known for midnight screenings, audience participation and songs including "The Time Warp."

Curry also was known for playing Pennywise in the 1990 miniseries "It," Wadsworth in "Clue," the concierge in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York" and the villainous Cardinal Richelieu in "The Three Musketeers."

His career spanned theater, film and television. Curry earned three Tony Award nominations for "My Favorite Year," "Amadeus" and "Spamalot." He won a Daytime Emmy Award, and also received a Primetime Emmy nomination.
"I like playing the more curious corners of the human mind and human behavior, partly because they’re a tad more interesting," Curry told the Associated Press in 1993.
'HOME ALONE' STAR CATHERINE O'HARA DEAD AT 71
Tim Curry, nominee for best performance by a leading actor in a musical for "Monty Python's Spamalot."  (Robin Platzer/FilmMagic/Getty Images)
The British actor had a major stroke in 2012 that left him using a wheelchair. He continued working in voice acting and returned to live-action film in 2024 with "Stream."
Curry was born in Cheshire, England, the son of a Navy chaplain and a school secretary. His father died when Curry was 12.
He discovered acting as a teenager and studied at the University of Birmingham before heading to London, where he landed his first West End job in "Hair."
"I took an academic course, which I largely ignored, I’m afraid, and just acted all the time," he said to the Associated Press.
His work with the Royal Shakespeare Company and Royal Court Theatre eventually led to "The Rocky Horror Show."

From right to left, actors Richard O'Brien, Tim Curry and Patricia Quinn as Riff Raff, Dr. Frank-N-Furter and Magenta from the 1975 musical comedy "The Rocky Horror Picture Show", produced by 20th Century Fox. ( Movie Poster Image Art/Getty Images)
In his 2025 memoir, "Vagabond," Curry reflected on the difference between his private life and the characters he played.

"The distinctions between who I really am and who I've pretended to be as an actor have proven to be a source of great disappointment to some audiences. It has not caused me much personal distress beyond the periodic necessity to deter stalkers," he wrote.
NEW ZEALAND ACTOR SAM NEILL DIES AT AGE 78 AFTER CANCER RECOVERY, FAMILY SAYS
Tim Curry as William Shakespeare appearing in the miniseries "Will Shakespeare." (David James /Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
Following news of Curry’s death, tributes began pouring in from fellow actors who remembered the actor and the iconic characters he created.

Michael McKean, who proudly called Curry his friend, shared on X, "My last conversation with Tim Curry was about life and love and laughter. The grim physical state he found himself in has now ended, a blessing. Our blessing was that we had Tim Curry in our lives. RIP, my friend."
Tim Curry, the one-of-a-kind star behind "Clue," "It" and "Annie" has died at 80. (Djamilla Rosa Cochran/WireImage)
Luke Evans, who recently played Frank-N-Furter on Broadway, revealed he had written Curry a letter just three weeks ago.
"There will only be one Tim Curry," Evans wrote, describing him as "a force, a bright fierce flame" and an inspiration.
"I hope, wherever you are, you’d approve of one more Frank having the time of his life in those heels," Evans wrote in part.
Lesley Ann Warren, Curry’s "Clue" co-star, called him "the brilliant, hilarious, hysterically funny, magician of artistry."
"I adored him. Bless his wild and inspired soul. Love you Tim," she wrote.
Actor Tim Curry attends the premiere of "The Rocky Horror Picture Show: Let's Do The Time Warp Again" at The Roxy Theatre on October 13, 2016. (Jason LaVeris/FilmMagic/Getty Images)
Fellow British actor Robin Askwith also paid tribute to Curry on X, writing, "RIP Tim Curry. Seems like yesterday Royal Court Upstairs. Seriously good….."

The official Muppets account also remembered Curry's performance as Long John Silver in 1996's "Muppet Treasure Island."

"Few humans have earned the title of honorary Muppet more than the legendary Tim Curry. As a performer he was unparalleled – witty, charming, unnerving, and deeply funny," the Instagram account wrote.
Tim Curry's career spanned theater, film and television. (Dimitrios Kambouris/WireImage for GLAAD)
"We will always consider it one of our greatest treasures to have been part of Long John Silver’s crew. Thank you for everything, Tim."

"The Parent Trap" star Elaine Hendrix wrote on social media, "And the blows keep coming. I worked with Tim Curry in the 90s. He was THE kindest man. I adored him up close and from a far since discovering ‘The Rocky Horror Picture Show’ while I was in High School. I was a huge fan of him! What a talent. What a gentleman. What an honor. RIP Tim"

Ireland Baldwin wrote on Instagram, "Two of my biggest inspirations passed away at 80. Crazy how their presence as performers led me to believe that they are immortal and couldn't possibly ever be gone. Fly HIGH above this crazy world."

The legendary actor never married and had no children. He remained private about his personal life while continuing to connect with fans through his work.

title: Dolly Parton's life in her own words: from Smoky Mountains poverty to country music immortality
summary: Dolly Parton's life in her own words reveals her Smoky Mountains childhood, faith, marriage to Carl Dean and her views on aging and what comes after.
story: Fox News senior national correspondent William La Jeunesse goes through the legacy of country music legend Dolly Parton on 'The Story.'

Country music icon Dolly Parton died peacefully in Nashville on Tuesday at 80 years old. Parton's team shared a statement with Fox News Digital on Tuesday night and confirmed that she died after a "brief battle with cancer."

Parton's death sparked mourning across the world. Parton’s catalog included enduring hits such as "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "Here You Come Again," "9 to 5" and "I Will Always Love You." The latter song became a global phenomenon again when Whitney Houston recorded it for 1992’s "The Bodyguard."

Throughout the span of her career, which ignited as a performer on "The Porter Wagoner Show," Parton always shared what mattered most to her – her Tennessee upbringing, her faith, her beloved husband, Carl Dean, and family.
Dolly Parton passed away peacefully on Tuesday. (Shirlaine Forrest/WireImage)
Below is a look at Parton's life, in her own words, over the years.
DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80
Smoky Mountains upbringing
Born in 1946 in rural Sevier County, Tennessee, Parton grew up in a large, poor family in the Smoky Mountains. She began singing in church as a child and started writing songs at a young age.
Dolly Parton in 1955. (Getty Images)

In 2015, Parton told Entertainment Tonight that her upbringing shaped who she became in her adult years. "I think my childhood made me everything I am today. I would trade nothing for being brought up in the Great Smoky Mountains. I’ve never been ashamed of my people no matter how poor or dirty we might have been," she said at the time.
Parton added, "I’ve always loved being from where I am, and having the folks that I’ve had."
During an interview with Rolling Stone in January, Parton shed a little more light on her poor childhood and said that her mother would make her clothes out of "feed sacks or scraps."
Country singer Dolly Parton in 1970. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
"We didn’t have anything. Mama used to sew all of our quilts and curtains for the windows, remake our clothes, and make clothes out of feed sacks or scraps," she said.
Parton was one of 12 children. Her parents were Robert Lee Parton Sr., known as Lee, a sharecropper and construction worker, and Avie Lee Caroline Parton, who raised their family.
Dolly's faith
Parton was very outspoken throughout her life about her Christian faith. During an interview with Fox News Digital in 2023, Parton said that her faith impacted everything she did.
GRAMMY-NOMINATED SINGER ANNE WILSON SAYS SPEAKING ABOUT JESUS COST HER OPPORTUNITIES, BUT SHE WON'T BACK DOWN

"My faith impacts everything I do because I do believe that, through God, all things are possible," she said at the time. "I always ask God to bless everything that I do and the people that I work with and to bring all the right things and right people into my life and to take the wrong ones out."
WATCH: Dolly Parton discusses the important role faith plays in her life
She added, "My spirituality has been a guiding light in my life and my strength, really, in my creative energy."
On the "WorkLife with Adam Grant" Ted Talk series in 2022, Parton shared that her religious beliefs were instilled in her at a young age.

"My grandpa was preacher. My mom was very religious, very spiritual. So I learned all the good lessons about loving your neighbor as yourself and judge not lest you be judged. Through God, all things are possible," she said.
WILLIE ROBERTSON'S FAITH-BASED ADVICE THAT'S KEPT HIS 34-YEAR MARRIAGE TO WIFE KORIE STRONG
WATCH: Dolly Parton: ‘I pray a lot and God's been really good to me'
Fox News looked back on Parton's history speaking about God in public. "I pray a lot and God's been really good to me," she said in March. In 2018, Parton said that music is "everything to me."
"It's my gift, it's my joy, it's my job," she continued.
Marriage to Carl Dean

Parton met Carl Dean outside the Wishy Washy Laundromat in Nashville on her first day in the city in 1964, when she was 18. They married two years later, on May 30, 1966, and remained together for nearly six decades until Dean’s death in 2025.
Dolly Parton and Carl Dean were married for nearly 60 years. (Dolly Parton Instagram)
After Dean died at the age of 82, the "Jolene" singer explained why she couldn't get herself to do what she loved: write songs.
DOLLY PARTON'S HUSBAND, CARL DEAN, DEAD AT 82

"I can’t afford the luxury of, you know, getting that emotional right now," she said during an appearance on Khloé Kardashian’s podcast, "Khloé in Wonder Land." "There are times like that, things like that, that will stall you a little bit. But I’ll write something else though, if it comes."
"I’m just putting that all on hold," Parton said.
Also, shortly after Dean's death, Parton told People that she would always keep him close to her heart.

"Ours is a great old love story. Most people don’t stay that close that long. That’s a loss. Nobody can ever know that unless you’ve experienced it yourself. He will always be in my heart and in my memories," she said.
Speaking to Fox News Digital in 2023, Parton said that part of the reason she believes their marriage lasted as long as it did was because she kept it private.
WATCH: Dolly Parton shares the secret to her long-time marriage

"The fact that he's not in show business at all, so we're not in competition on that. We don't have to deal with it. He's kind of a homebody. He loves working on the farm. He loves workin' on his tractors and his trucks and all that. He was in asphalt paving for years, and then he went into kinda doin' some real estate. But he don't wanna be in the spotlight, but he's very proud of and for me," she said at the time.

"When I first won an award, when we first married in '66... he just started taking clothes off before we even got out of the building. Before we got to the car, he had that bowtie off from that tuxedo. Had that shirt, jacket off, and he said, 'I want you to be successful. Do whatever you want to do, but leave me out of this. I ain't doing any more of these things, so don't ask me.' So I never did it," Parton said.
Shortly after Dead died, Parton told The Associated Press that she "truly believe[s] that I’m going to see him again someday."
Dolly's legacy
Parton built a seven-decade career as a singer, songwriter, actress, author, businesswoman and philanthropist, winning 11 Grammy Awards and becoming one of country music’s most enduring stars.
Beyond music, she created Dollywood, founded the Imagination Library and brought her larger-than-life personality to films including "9 to 5" and "Steel Magnolias."
Dolly Parton in a publicity picture for the movie "Rhinestone" in 1984. (Getty Images)
In 2025, Parton spoke to People about how she was able to not only maintain a country music career, but crossover to Hollywood successfully and find the time for her charitable efforts.

"I don’t try to tell other people how to do it, how to be, but I know who I am. I’m a star to everybody but me. I’m just a working girl. I always just say that I’m a workhorse that looks like a show horse," she said at the time.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I’m at that point in my life where I just want to be able to do good things that can be carried on. I’m proud of my legacy so far, and I hope to just continue to do things that might be of use to other people," Parton added.
Parton died on August 25 at the age of 80. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
In 2022, Parton said part of the reason she found the time to do the things she loved was because she didn't sleep much.

"I don’t need a whole lot of sleep," the singer insisted to Insider. "I go to bed pretty early, but even if I’ve been up late – it’s just kind of like a little clock inside of me that says, ‘It’s 3 o’clock!’"
"I do some of my best work there, but I get enough sleep. I don’t require as much sleep as a lot of other people do. That’s kind of a Parton family trait," she continued.
Parton's stance on aging
After Parton turned 77 in 2023, she spoke to Insider about how she viewed getting older.
The singer said she's come to terms with the idea that "wisdom comes with age, and you can't stop the aging process, nor the numbers."
Dolly Parton passed away on Tuesday, August 25 at 80. (Getty Images)
DOLLY PARTON SAYS SHE’D ‘RATHER BE’ IN HER 70S THAN BE YOUNG AGAIN: ‘I MEAN THIS FROM THE BOTTOM OF MY HEART’

"Honestly — and I mean this from the bottom of my heart — when I see young people today and I see what they're going to have to go through, especially in this day and time, I would honestly rather be this age than that age," Parton explained.

The legendary singer acknowledged she's no different from "everyone (who) would like to stay 35 forever," but she doesn't spend her life thinking about her age and doesn't let it get in the way of her doing what she wants.
Parton performed at the halftime show at the Dallas Cowboys’ Thanksgiving Day game in 2023, dressed as a Dallas Cowboy Cheerleader. (Ron Jenkins/Getty Images)

"The way I live, the way I work, the way I feel, I'm going to make every moment count," Parton said. "I may live to be 100 or I may die tomorrow, but whenever that is, I will know I died trying, and I will know I've done everything I could to make the most of everything."
"As long as I stay healthy, the numbers shouldn't matter. I don't feel my age, I don't work my age, I don't think my age and, hopefully, I don't look my age," she noted.
"I may live to be 100 or I may die tomorrow, but whenever that is, I will know I died trying, and I will know I've done everything I could to make the most of everything."
Just before her 80th birthday this year, Parton told People that she felt like she was "just getting started."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"If you allow yourself to get old, you will. People say, ‘How come you don’t seem to get old?’ I say, ‘I ain’t got time to get old,’" she said. "I ain’t got time to dwell on that. That’s not what I’m thinking about," she told the outlet.
What Dolly believed came after death
In 2019, Parton shared rare comments on what she believed would happen after she died during an episode of the "Dolly Parton's America" podcast.
Dolly Parton believed in life after death. (Getty Images)

"As far as what happens after we go on, like I say, I’m no saint so I’m hoping just as a Christian faith person, that we go on to a greater thing. I believe that we’re all part of that great divine plan, and I’m hoping to get on up there, and do some more writing, and singing, and playing with those golden harps, and write some more songs, and have my own mansion, and walk them golden streets of glory, and keep doing it forever and ever and ever.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
"So I’m going to get in the angel band, for sure. I want to play in the angel band and I want to maybe play the harp up there. I don’t know," she said.
Dolly Parton appeared on the Phil Donahue Show in 1977. (Getty Images)
On the podcast, Parton said that she "kind of" believed in reincarnation and was "open to things."

"You just hope and you have faith. That’s what faith is. But I believe that it’s going to be better. I think it’s not the end of me. I don’t think it’s the end of any of us. I think we’re recycled and if nothing else, we just go back into that great flow of divine energy, and hopefully we can spread ourselves around in other wonderful ways. That’s what I hope," Parton said.

title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle won’t ‘hijack’ Prince George’s historic Eton debut, royal expert says
summary: Royal experts say Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will likely "lay low" when Prince George starts at Eton College this September.
story: Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair royal correspondent and co-host of "The Royals Uncensored," says Prince George passed Eton's admissions process like other applicants before accepting his place at the prestigious school.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are expected to steer clear of releasing photos, making comments or generating other news that could overshadow Prince George’s highly anticipated first day at Eton College, according to a royal expert.

"The Sussexes have assured the king that they will not hijack or derail major royal events, notably the first day of school term for Prince George at Eton," royal broadcaster Neil Sean told Fox News Digital. "By that, no pictures or comment from either one on that day in September."
A representative for Archewell told Fox News Digital: "This is not something we would comment on." Kensington Palace did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The reported understanding comes as the Prince and Princess of Wales prepare for a major family milestone. Kensington Palace confirmed in June that George, 13, will attend Eton beginning this September, following in the footsteps of both his father, Prince William, and his uncle, Harry.
PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON WRESTLED WITH MAJOR DECISION OVER PRINCE GEORGE'S FUTURE: EXPERT
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle won’t "hijack" Prince George’s start at Eton, according to a royal expert. (Getty Images)
Royal commentator Amanda Matta told Fox News Digital that George’s arrival at the prestigious boarding school carries significance beyond a typical first day.

"Prince George’s start at Eton isn’t just a personal milestone; it’s the beginning of his public-facing path as heir to the throne," Matta said. "The Palace is incredibly protective of that narrative, and any competing headline — especially one involving Harry and Meghan — threatens to distract from the ‘steady, future-focused’ brand the Prince and Princess of Wales have worked so hard to build."
PRINCE WILLIAM ‘BLINDSIDED’ BY HARRY, MEGHAN RETURN AS KATE FEARS NEW TURMOIL FROM ROYAL FEUD: EXPERTS
She added that, while the matter may not weigh heavily on Prince William and Kate Middleton personally, it could be important to palace staff working to keep the focus on the future king.
Prince George of Wales is said to be excited that he'll be attending Eton College in the fall. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
"It would certainly be a shame for his first days at Eton to see him embroiled in a ‘feud’ narrative with his uncle and aunt," Matta said.

In a statement shared with The New York Times last week, a spokesperson for the Sussexes said, "On the heels of a wonderful trip with family and friends this summer, Harry and Meghan have decided to spend an extended period in the U.K. this autumn. They are excited to have their children spend more time in the country that’s such an important part of their family’s story."

The spokesperson confirmed that the couple’s businesses will remain unchanged and based in the U.S. Meghan and Harry will also keep their home in California.

Matta said the reported agreement may reflect an informal attempt to avoid competing headlines during significant occasions, though the couple's public profile makes a complete break from the royal news cycle unlikely.
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex will be returning to the U.K. this fall. (Chris Jackson - Pool/Getty Images)
