title: Chinese humanoid robot breaks Usain Bolt's 100m dash record at 9.39 seconds
summary: A humanoid robot named Lightning Bolt ran 100 meters in 9.39 seconds at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, edging Usain Bolt's record.
story: A Chinese robot beat Usain Bolt’s 100-meter mark as humanoids raced, kicked soccer balls, boxed and danced at a major robotics showcase. (Credit: Associated Press)
The world's fastest man record was shattered on the first day of the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday.

Jamaican Usain Bolt's 100-meter dash record of 9.58 set in 2009 was edged by a Beijing-based X-Humanoid robot named Lightning Bolt, which ran 100 meters at 9:39 seconds before smashing into a blue wall.

Before the opening, a humanoid robot from Chinese smartphone company Honor completed a 100-meter sprint in a record of 9.32 seconds during a trial of the games, the company said, at a peak speed of 14.5 meters per second.
After smashing into the wall, the robots were placed on a stretcher, unlike Bolt, who was able to jog a lap to celebrate human achievement in 2009.
ROBOTS BEAT HUMANS IN HALF MARATHON

Spectators watch as a Lightning humanoid robot by Honor and a Tiangong Ultra humanoid robot compete in a 100-meter exhibition race during the opening ceremony for the second World Humanoid Robot Games at the National Speed Skating Oval in Beijing, China, on Aug. 22, 2026. (Florence Lo/Reuters)

The World Humanoid Robot Games, in its second year, features more than 2,000 robots in 51 events and 1,000 competitions like running, table tennis and soccer. The five-day event highlights China's rapid progress in robotics amid a heated tech race with the U.S.

The games, which are taking place in the National Speed Skating Oval built for the 2022 Winter Olympics, opened the same week Beijing was holding the 2026 World Robot Conference, where companies showcased around 3,000 products, including humanoid robots.
CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE
Humanoid robots show they can beat the world's fastest man reach in the 100-meter dash, but they cannot stop without a blue wall. (Tingshu Wang/Reuters)

In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88 meters, well above the 0.95 meters best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45 meters set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993.
Some spectators at the robot games said they were excited about the humanoid robots’ quickly improving abilities.
Humanoid robots are "evolving rapidly," said Li Yanfeng, an education worker and a Beijing resident.
UNITREE G1 HUMANOID ROBOT ICE SKATES AND ROLLERBLADES
Staff members move the humanoid robots onto stretchers after they crashed into the blue-cushioned wall at the National Speed Skating Oval in Beijing, China, on Aug. 22, 2026. (Florence Lo/Reuters)

"At first, I wasn’t very accepting of artificial intelligence. I was even a bit resistant to it, because of the possibility that it might replace or displace humans," she said. "But now that I see this development is unstoppable, I decided to come and take a look."
"These sports are perfectly normal for humans, but now robots can do them. I find it amazing," said Yang Shangzheng, another spectator.
NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL
Liu Tao, who was watching the games with his son, said he was hoping to see "the best robots China currently has to offer."
This year’s robot games — which the organizer said has 16 countries participating, among them Germany, Japan and the U.S. — also include other events such as weightlifting and tug of war.
Jamaican Usain Bolt ran the 100-meter dash in 9.58 seconds in 2009. (AP Photo)
The U.S. has stepped up scrutiny of robots from China, which makes the majority of the world's humanoid robots.

President Donald Trump's Federal Communications Commission (FCC) banned imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots, because they "pose unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States or the safety and security of United States persons."

"I welcome these Executive Branch national security determinations, and I am pleased that the FCC has now added foreign produced advanced robotics and power inverters to the FCC’s Covered List," FCC Chair Brendan Carr wrote in a statement last month. "Following President Trump’s leadership, the FCC will continue to do our part to secure America’s critical supply chains and, with today’s action, the FCC is acting in lock step with our national security agencies to do just that."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: AI agent hacks gym system to move up waitlist
summary: An AI agent using Claude AI canceled another person's gym booking after finding a security flaw in the reservation system's authorization checks.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Booking a gym class seems like exactly the kind of everyday task you might hand over to an AI agent. But when Andrew Bird did that in Australia, his AI assistant found a way around the gym's booking rules and took an action he never explicitly asked it to take. What happened next is a good example of why giving AI agents more freedom can come with some very real risks.

No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.
Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI KILL SWITCH BILL COULD SHUT DOWN ROGUE MODELS
Andrew Bird turned to an AI agent to help him get into a popular Pilates class, but the booking task went much further than he expected. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How the AI agent gym hack happened

Bird, head of AI at Australian software company Affinda, had been experimenting with OpenClaw, AI agent software running with Anthropic's Claude AI service. He wanted the agent to take care of booking a popular gym class.

The agent discovered that the booking software did not properly enforce some restrictions. It found a way to reserve classes several weeks beyond the intended booking window. Later, Bird was fourth on a waitlist for a class. He asked whether the agent could move him to the top.

The agent discovered another weakness. The booking system lacked authorization checks that should have prevented one user from canceling another person's reservation. Then the agent tested that weakness on the person sitting at the top of the waitlist. The cancellation worked. Bird moved from fourth to third. He did not move into the class, and he did not even reach the top of the waitlist.
Bird had asked whether moving higher was possible. He had not instructed the agent to remove another person to make that happen.
The AI removed another person from the waitlist

That sequence is important because the agent was not following a command to cancel someone else's reservation. It found its own method for pursuing Bird's goal. After the cancellation, Bird immediately asked the AI to undo what it had done. The agent told him it could not add the person back and removed the person at the top of the waitlist.

That bumped Bird from No. 4 to No. 3. What gets my attention is how it got there. The agent found a security weakness and tested it on a real person's waitlist entry without Bird explicitly asking it to do that.
The booking software also failed

The AI agent deserves scrutiny here, but the booking software had a serious weakness too. A properly secured reservation system should not let one account cancel another person's reservation simply because someone sends the right request to its application programming interface, or API. The agent reported that the API lacked authorization checks for canceling other people's reservations.

That weakness gave the AI an opening. This is worth watching as AI agents become more capable. They can interact with websites and online services that may contain weak authorization controls or other security flaws. A human might see a full class and stop. An AI agent may keep looking for another route.
LOCK DOWN YOUR CHATGPT ACCOUNT BEFORE THE NEXT AI ATTACK
The AI agent found a security weakness in the gym's booking system and used it while trying to complete Bird's request. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Bird reports the security flaw

After the agent failed to restore the other gym member's place, Bird focused on getting the vulnerability reported. He asked the AI to prepare a responsible disclosure email for the gym software provider. The agent drafted the message and sent it back to Bird for approval.

The Australian news outlet reported that the company behind the booking software declined to discuss specific security issues. Anthropic did not respond to the outlet's request for comment. CyberGuy also reached out to Anthropic for comment, but did not hear back before our deadline.
AI agents can take action for you

A chatbot typically waits for a question and gives you an answer. An AI agent can do much more. Depending on the setup, it can interact with websites and use connected tools to complete multistep tasks. That capability can save a lot of time.

You could ask an agent to research travel options or handle a repetitive online task without walking it through every click. But greater freedom also gives the AI more choices about how it reaches your goal.

That raises a harder question. What happens when an agent finds a method that technically works but crosses a boundary you never intended it to cross? Bird's gym experience gives us a very relatable example. He wanted help with a booking. The agent discovered a software weakness and used it in a way that affected another person.
Why AI agents are raising bigger security questions

The gym episode comes as researchers and AI companies examine what happens when powerful AI systems encounter obstacles while pursuing a goal. The Australian report pointed to recent cybersecurity evaluations in which advanced AI models reached real systems they were not supposed to access.

Those situations involved deliberate security testing. Bird's case stands out because it happened during an everyday task, outside a cybersecurity evaluation. AI agents are increasingly being given access to websites and connected services. If those systems contain weak authorization controls, capable agents may find them.
Why this AI gym hack should get your attention

Websites contain bugs. Weak permissions and poorly secured APIs are nothing new. What is changing is the software interacting with them. An AI agent can keep trying different approaches after the obvious route fails. It can inspect available tools and work through a problem without waiting for you to direct every step. That can be incredibly useful when the agent stays within the boundaries you intended.

The concern comes when it decides for itself which methods are acceptable. Bird wanted to move up a gym waitlist. His agent found an option Bird never explicitly authorized. Now think about the same behavior involving your email, financial accounts or other sensitive services. The stakes rise quickly.
The incident shows why AI agents need clear limits before they are given permission to act on your behalf. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to keep control when using AI agents
AI agents can make tedious tasks easier, but I would be careful about how much authority you hand over.

Give an AI agent access only to the accounts it needs for the job. Avoid connecting sensitive accounts simply because the option exists. More access gives an agent more places where an unexpected action can have consequences.

Whenever the tool allows it, require your approval before the agent sends messages, spends money or changes a reservation. You want to see a consequential action before it happens rather than discovering it afterward.

Do not focus only on the result you want. Tell the agent what methods are off-limits. For example, you could say: "Only use options normally available to me. Do not bypass restrictions, exploit security weaknesses or change another person's account or reservation." That gives the AI clearer instructions about how you expect it to behave.

Test an agent with tasks where a mistake will not cost you money or affect another person. Then watch how it completes those jobs. The final result is only part of the story. The steps the agent takes to get there can tell you much more.

If your AI tool shows its activity history, check it. An agent may deliver exactly what you requested while using a method you never would have approved yourself. Bird's gym experience shows why that oversight is worth the extra minute.
Kurt's key takeaways

What gets me about this story is how normal Bird's request was. He wanted an AI agent to help him get into a gym class. He was not asking it to break into software or remove somebody from a waitlist. Then the agent found a weakness and used it while trying to accomplish his goal. The booking platform clearly had a security problem. One user should not have been able to remove another person's reservation that way. At the same time, AI agents introduce a new concern. They can keep searching for another way to get something done when the obvious route does not work. I like the idea of an AI assistant taking tedious jobs off my plate. But I want to know when it is about to cross a line I never told it to cross. That becomes much more serious when an agent has access to my email, money or an important account. For now, I would keep a human approval step between an AI agent and any action that could affect somebody else or create a consequence you cannot easily undo.

title: Mica Miller’s siblings allege pastor husband forced final hospitalization before her 2024 death
summary: Mica Miller's siblings allege JP Miller had her involuntarily committed as part of a coercive control pattern during their troubled marriage.
story: South Carolina woman Mica Miller, found dead in Lumber River State Park on April 27, called 911 in the moments before her death, according to the Robeson County Sheriff's Office. (Credit: Robeson County Sheriff's Office)
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Mica Miller's siblings are speaking out about the late worship leader's troubled marriage, alleging her estranged husband, South Carolina pastor John-Paul "JP" Miller, had her involuntarily admitted to a mental-health facility.

Mica’s family discusses the alleged hospitalization in "Death of the Pastor’s Wife," a three-part true-crime series that premiered Wednesday on Netflix. The documentary delves into her life, marriage and April 2024 death, which authorities ruled a suicide.
Mica’s family describes the hospitalization as part of a broader alleged pattern of coercive control during her marriage.
SC PASTOR'S WIFE MICA MILLER TOLD POLICE SHE WAS BEING TRACKED BEFORE HER SUICIDE: DOCS

Mica Miller was found dead in the water with an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, and the gun was located nearby, on April 27. 2024. The North Carolina Medical Examiner’s Office later ruled the death a suicide. (Courtesy of Netflix)
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Her final hospitalization was involuntary, the siblings allege. They claim Miller contacted a mental-health facility and initiated the admission against his wife’s wishes.

According to her siblings, Mica was diagnosed with bipolar disorder while she was engaged to Miller, who reportedly took an active role in overseeing her care. They claim she was hospitalized multiple times during the relationship, including shortly before the couple married in 2017.
Left: John-Paul Miller and Mica Miller. Right: John-Paul Miller after an arrest. (Facebook)
In a handwritten affidavit accompanying her divorce filing reviewed by Fox News Digital, Mica alleged that she had been abused "emotionally, sexually, spiritually, financially, and physically."

The family further said that while Mica was hospitalized, Miller took possession of her vehicle, phone and laptop. Her siblings said the computer contained intimate photographs of her. Mica later reported the alleged incident to police, according to the Netflix series.
Miller reportedly declined to participate in the documentary. Fox News Digital has reached out to his attorneys for comment.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
According to Netflix, the docu-series "Death of the Pastor’s Wife" features never-before-seen footage and firsthand accounts from friends and family. (Courtesy of Netflix)
The documentary relies on interviews with Mica’s relatives, friends, former Solid Rock Church members and divorce attorney, the streaming platform said.

Mica, 30, was found dead at Lumber River State Park in North Carolina on April 27, 2024, two days after serving Miller with divorce papers.

The Robeson County Sheriff’s Office concluded that she died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound and closed its investigation. Miller has denied involvement in her death and has not been charged in connection with it.
Mica Miller and her husband, John Paul Miller, served with Solid Rock Church in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. (Courtesy of Netflix)

He is, however, facing an unrelated federal prosecution over his alleged conduct toward Mica before her death.

A federal grand jury indicted Miller in December 2025 on charges of cyberstalking and making false statements to investigators, according to a release from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of South Carolina on Dec. 18, 2025.

Prosecutors allege that he posted a nude photograph of Mica online without her consent, had tracking devices placed on her vehicle, contacted her more than 50 times in one day, interfered with her finances and damaged her tires.
READ THE INDICTMENT:

Miller's alleged cyberstalking put his wife in "reasonable fear of death and serious bodily injury," according to the federal indictment, which added that his conduct "would be reasonably expected to cause [Mica Miller] substantial emotional distress."

Federal authorities say that Miller also lied to investigators when he was questioned about damaging Mica's tires. Investigators later found that Miller purchased a tire-deflation device online and sent messages to others referencing her vehicle, according to the indictment.

If convicted, Miller could face a maximum sentence of five years in prison on the cyberstalking charge and two years for making false statements, along with fines of up to $250,000. Miller pleaded not guilty and remains free on a $100,000 bond.
MICA MILLER 911 CALL REVEALS FINAL MOMENTS BEFORE HER DEATH AS NC AUTHORITIES CHALLENGE ‘CONSPIRACY THEORIES’

Following weekly protests from domestic violence advocates and an FBI investigation into J.P. Miller, Solid Rock Church in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina was permanently closed in November 2024. (Courtesy of Netflix)

title: Strange Georgia crime-scene clues blow hole in theory of mom’s mysterious death, family says
summary: Natalie Jones' toxicology report came back clean, yet Georgia authorities pushed an overdose theory before closing her 2020 Heard County death case.
story: Internet searches from conman Brian Walshe and voicemails from his mother, Diana, take center stage in new Fox Nation special on the Ana Walshe murder case.
A negative toxicology report, missing teeth and an unusually positioned driver’s seat are fueling renewed questions into the unexplained 2020 death of Georgia mother Natalie Jones.
"The Truth About Natalie," a six-part Audiochuck series, examines the 27-year-old’s life before her disappearance, the circumstances surrounding her death and a questionable overdose theory.
The series draws from case files, crime-scene evidence, candid interviews with family members and a volunteer advocate, along with independent forensic analysis.
Jones’ mother, Elaine Gordon, told Fox News Digital that friction with investigators began during the search. She alleged that a detective accused her of interfering as she pressed for answers.
Natalie Jones was found dead in Georgia in 2020. (Courtesy of Elaine Gordon)
DETECTIVES' TRUE CRIME PODCAST TAKES FRESH SHOT AT KILLER WHO VANISHED AFTER CAUGHT-ON-CAMERA MURDER

"What did they expect me to do, sit at home and be quiet? And I still want somebody to answer this for me: How do we even know Natalie left that lake house in the first place?" Gordon told Fox News Digital.
Gordon also questioned whether investigators thoroughly interviewed everyone connected to her daughter’s final hours.
The final text

Jones disappeared after reportedly leaving a friend’s lake house in Jackson’s Gap, Alabama, on July 4, 2020, in a bright pink 2002 Chevrolet Cavalier. She planned to drive home to Heard County, Georgia.
At 12:52 a.m. the following morning, her phone sent its last outgoing text to the mother of a former boyfriend.
Natalie Jones' family wants answers as questions remain about how she died in Georgia. (Courtesy of Elaine Gordon)
"I made it. Thanks."
The message did not indicate where Jones had arrived.

Cellphone data reviewed in the podcast indicated that on July 5, Jones’ phone connected with towers across Heard County in a scattered pattern, including on the opposite side of the county from her home. Cellular activity stopped shortly after 5 a.m.
Later that morning, Jones failed to arrive at her sister’s home to babysit her children, prompting the family to contact police.
Nearly three months passed without answers. Then, in October 2020, a property owner’s nephew discovered Jones’ vehicle off Roosterville Road in rural Heard County, covered in thick vegetation.
Natalie Jones is pictured with one of her sons. (Courtesy of Elaine Gordon)
UC DAVIS FRATERNITY STUDENT'S 2001 DEATH RULED A SUICIDE AFTER 29 STAB WOUNDS QUESTIONED IN TRUE CRIME PODCAST

Heard County Sheriff’s Office deputies found Jones deceased in the driver’s seat, slumped toward the driver’s side door, wearing the same clothes she had worn to the gathering. Her body showed advanced decomposition and partial mummification.
The medical examiner could not determine Jones’ cause or manner of death.
GOLDEN STATE KILLER INVESTIGATOR FINDS ‘RED FLAGS’ IN MARILYN MONROE DEATH SCENE DECADES LATER
Questions inside the car
Although investigators said they found no evidence of foul play, the podcast highlighted several details that left Jones’ family scrambling for answers.

Crime-scene photos showed the driver’s seat reclined and pushed farther back than Jones, who stood 5 feet, 5 inches tall, would have kept it. Strands of her hair were wedged along the driver-side door jamb, and the vehicle’s trunk had been popped open.
Natalie Jones was 27 when she died. (Courtesy of Elaine Gordon)
Jones’ cellphone, rhinestone sandals, belt and white sunglasses were unaccounted for. Several of her teeth were also missing.
Investigators found a small bag inside the car, possibly containing methamphetamine, but the GBI Crime Lab recovered no fingerprints from it. Jones’ toxicology screening came back negative for drugs.
Family seeks new review

In 2021, family advocate Jennifer Peterson petitioned the Heard County Superior Court to impanel a special grand jury to examine Jones’ death, including the possible involvement of a former boyfriend who had been identified as a person of interest, but never charged in the case.
In 2022, the district attorney told Peterson that the case was being closed.
"We have raised serious questions, inconsistencies and concerns, and too often it feels like they are dismissed, minimized or ignored," Peterson told Fox News Digital.
By 2023, law enforcement and the district attorney’s office had stopped responding to her, Peterson said.
Natalie Jones wanted a better life for herself and her two sons, her mother said. (Courtesy of Elaine Gordon)
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"At some point, you have to ask, ‘Who polices the police?’ And what does it take for someone with the authority to simply say, ‘I’ll listen, I’ll look at it, and I’ll help?’ We are still waiting for that person. Hopefully, someone can help us."
Peterson contacted Audiochuck podcast host Sean Kipe in March 2023.
"What bothers me most is that authorities pushed an accidental overdose theory even though Natalie’s toxicology report came back completely clean," Kipe told Fox News Digital.
"Combining that negative drug test with missing evidence like her phone, shoes and teeth makes it nearly impossible to accept the official explanation."
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Kipe said Heard County authorities have not contacted him since the podcast’s release. He added, however, that several law enforcement officers from the area reached out to him with doubts about the overdose theory.
The Heard County Sheriff’s Office told Fox News Digital that investigators are still seeking leads in the case and that if "anything comes in, we will be glad to run it down."
The Heard County DA’s Office referred the inquiry to the West Georgia Judicial Circuit DA’s Office, which was not immediately available for comment.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
"My ultimate hope is to bring Natalie’s mother and children the closure they deserve after years of unanswered questions," Kipe said.
SEND US A TIP
"By sharing this story with a wide audience, we want to compel authorities to reopen the investigation into Natalie’s death and encourage anyone with information about the case to come forward."
GOT A TIP?
Natalie Jones is pictured with her mother, Elaine Gordon. (Courtesy of Elaine Gordon)
For Gordon, the podcast also offers an opportunity to show listeners who her daughter was beyond the unanswered questions surrounding her death.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
"I want everybody to know how loved Natalie was and how much she loved her boys, Trent and Isaac. She wanted a better life for the three of them," Gordon said. "She was excited about her future."
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Gordon said that before she disappeared, Jones had bought land and was planning to build a home there for her two young sons. She also had plans to attend college.

title: Fox Hollow coroner reveals why he doubts suspected serial killer acted alone in hunt for answers
summary: Over 9,000 bones remain unexamined at Fox Hollow Farm as the true crime documentary explores whether suspected serial killer Herb Baumeister acted alone.
story: The Indiana coroner leading an investigation to identify the victims of the alleged Fox Hollow Farm serial killer said that "several tragedies" still remain.

Nearly 30 years after thousands of human bones and bone fragments were unearthed at the sprawling estate of suspected serial killer Herb Baumeister, new questions are being raised about the mystery of what really happened at Fox Hollow Farm.
The coroner leading the renewed investigation claims a key figure in the case has not been fully forthcoming with investigators.
"I have had an opportunity to speak with Mark Goodyear a couple of times," Hamilton County Coroner Jeff Jellison told Fox News Digital.
FOX HOLLOW FARM SERIAL KILLER'S 10TH VICTIM IDENTIFIED: CORONER
Hamilton County coroner Jeff Jellison's mission is to identify the remains from Fox Hollow Farm. (ABC News Studios)

"The first question I would ask him is, ‘Are you ready to be honest with me?’ Because in the conversations we’ve had, he’s not been honest. I’ve asked him questions that I knew the answer to, and he didn’t pass that test. So for me to sit down with Mark Goodyear, he’s going to have to be willing to be honest in this conversation. I don’t have time to sit down with somebody that tells lies, untruths."
Authorities dig for human bones in a wooded area on the Fox Hollow Farm in Westfield. (Rich Miller/Indy Star-USA TODAY NETWORK/Imagn)

Jellison appears in the ABC News Studios true crime documentary "Return to Fox Hollow: New Victims, Darker Secrets," which explores new theories about potential accomplices, overlooked evidence and witness accounts in the case of Baumeister, a suspected serial killer believed to have murdered numerous men in Indiana. It's a follow-up to the 2025 docuseries "The Fox Hollow Murders: Playground of a Serial Killer."
Jellison said he wants to determine whether Goodyear knows something that could help investigators identify the remaining victims and determine how they died.
Indiana resident Herb Baumeister was suspected of killing at least 25 victims. (Indianapolis Police Department)
Goodyear has never been charged with any crime related to the case and has repeatedly denied any involvement in the disappearances.

"If we move forward in that conversation, certainly I want to know any information I can gather to help identify these remains," said Jellison. "Were you familiar with anybody? Things that would focus more around identification and how these people died."
A portrait of Jeffery Allen Jones, who was identified as a victim of suspected serial killer Herb Baumeister. (Michelle Pemberton/IndyStar / USA TODAY NETWORK/Imagn)
"Mark Goodyear knows a lot about this case," Jellison said.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Mark Goodyear was questioned by Hamilton County police in 1996. He claimed to be Herb Baumeister’s sole survivor. (ABC News Studios)
Jellison also shared that Goodyear knew many people through gay nightclubs and could help investigators identify some of the remains.

Goodyear, who participated in the first docuseries, has described himself as Baumeister's only known survivor. The film detailed how investigators believed Baumeister may have filmed his victims with a secret camera hidden in an air vent in his basement. Goodyear said he was forced to watch some of the tapes in 1994. He said the video was so "bad" it made him scream.
A memorial stands at Prairie Waters Funeral and Event Center at Hamilton Memorial Park for the victims of suspected serial killer Herb Baumeister. (Michelle Pemberton/IndyStar / USA TODAY NETWORK)

"It was like having a camera right up against something," Goodyear said. "You're not going to be able to tell what's going on, but the minute you got a flash of what was going on, it made you scream."
"Return to Fox Hollow: New Victims, Darker Secrets" is available for streaming on Hulu and Hulu on Disney+. (ABC News Studios)

The previous documentary examined how Goodyear's account of his relationship and encounters with Baumeister has changed over the years. At the time, Jellison told Fox News Digital it was unlikely those tapes, if they exist, would ever be recovered.
Fox News Digital reached out to Goodyear for comment but did not receive a response.
Daniel Thomas Halloran's remains were identified after they were found at Fox Hollow Farm. (Michelle Pemberton/USA TODAY NETWORK/Imagn and Hamilton County Coroner's Office)
Goodyear initially agreed to another interview for the follow-up documentary but did not appear for the scheduled interview, according to the film.
SIGN UP TO GET THE TRUE CRIME NEWSLETTER
Mark Goodyear did not participate in "Return to Fox Hollow: New Victims, Darker Secrets." He left a voicemail for producers heard in the film. (ABC News Studios)

About 10,000 burned and broken human bones and bone fragments were recovered from the 18-acre estate that once belonged to Baumeister. Before investigators could arrest him in 1996, Baumeister was found dead of a self-inflicted gunshot wound in Ontario, Canada. He was 49.
Investigators believe Baumeister frequented gay bars in Indianapolis, lured men to his home while his family was away, killed them there and disposed of their remains on the property.
About 10,000 remains of Indiana serial killer Herb Baumeister were found on the 18-acre Westfield, Indiana, property. (Google Street View)
Baumeister's son discovered a human skull in the woods at Fox Hollow Farm in 1994, but, according to reports, investigators did not search the property until June 1996.
Fox Hollow Farm in Westfield, Indiana was once owned by suspected serial killer Herb Baumeister, owner of the Sav-a-Lot shopping chain. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Goodyear said he first encountered Baumeister at an Indianapolis gay bar in 1994, where Baumeister introduced himself as "Brian." Goodyear later told investigators that he went home with Baumeister and described what he said was a disturbing sexual encounter.

Goodyear's account eventually helped advance the investigation. After encountering Baumeister again the following year, Goodyear helped investigators obtain information that led them to identify Baumeister.
Evening view of the area behind the Fox Hill Farm main house. (Michelle Pemberton-USA TODAY NETWORK/Imagn)
While Jellison has questioned Goodyear's account, he also made clear in the documentary that Goodyear was not a suspect.
GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB

Hamilton County Coroner Jeff Jellison stands for the victims of the Fox Hollow Farm tragedy during services on Aug. 29, 2024, at Prairie Waters Funeral and Event Center at Hamilton Memorial Park in Westfield, Indiana. (Michelle Pemberton/IndyStar / USA TODAY NETWORK)
"There are very strong indications there is another suspect, and it wasn’t Mark Goodyear," Jellison said in the film.
Jellison said there are still more than 9,000 bones and bone fragments yet to be examined. Investigators believe at least 25 people fell victim to Baumeister, according to WRTV.

A photo of Allen Livingston sits next to his remains during the first public remembrance services for all nine identified Fox Hollow Farm victims on Aug. 29, 2024, at Prairie Waters Funeral and Event Center at Hamilton Memorial Park in Westfield, Indiana. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
The scope and placement of the remains have also raised another question for Jellison: whether Baumeister could have carried out the crimes alone.
Victims were identified in 2023 and 2024, thanks to efforts by Jeff Jellison. (Michelle Pemberton/IndyStar / USA TODAY NETWORK/Imagn)

"I was always convinced that there was more than one," Jellison said. "There were a lot of people that lost their lives in this incident, and just the placement of the evidence alone. How does one man pull this crime off? And how does one man get ... deceased individuals from his residence to potentially 200 yards through very dense woods? I think it would've been a very difficult task."
The sign at Fox Hollow Farm in Westfield, Indiana. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Jellison is determined to put names to the unidentified victims. He believes some families may still be unaware that a loved one vanished or that the person's remains may have ended up at Fox Hollow Farm.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Property owner Rob Graves points to the area behind his home where suspected serial killer Herb Baumeister may have dumped multiple bodies. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
Jellison compared the scale of the investigation to the recovery effort at the World Trade Center.

"Some of these folks did not have close family connections, and they were somewhat marginalized," he explained. "So there may be families out there not even knowing that their loved one went missing, much less consider that person was a victim at Fox Hollow."

title: Bryan Kohberger seeks judge’s removal in escalating bid to undo guilty plea
summary: Bryan Kohberger is seeking to withdraw his guilty plea for the murders of four University of Idaho students, arguing he was coerced into a false confession.
story: Dr. Kris Mohandie, a renowned forensic psychologist who predicted Bryan Kohberger would attempt to appeal his guilty plea last year, weighs in on Kohberger's ‘narcissism’ and latest legal move.

Bryan Kohberger, the man convicted of fatally stabbing four University of Idaho students, is asking a court to disqualify the judge in his case and has asked for a change of venue as he attempts to take back his guilty plea.
Motions for both requests were filed Thursday by Kohberger's new court-appointed attorney, Gregory Rauch. The move came after Kohberger was convicted of first-degree murder.
Kohberger has since claimed he is innocent and has blamed his defense team for leading him to make a false confession.
BRYAN KOHBERGER GETS NEW ATTORNEY APPOINTED AFTER HE ASKS COURT FOR POST-CONVICTION RELIEF IN IDAHO MURDERS

Bryan Kohberger appears at the Ada County Courthouse for his sentencing hearing July 23, 2025, in Boise, Idaho, for brutally stabbing four University of Idaho students to death. (AP Photo/Kyle Green, Pool)

The motions are asking for Fourth Judicial District Judge Steven Hippler to be disqualified for Kohberger's post-conviction court proceedings and for the hearings to be moved out of Ada County. The motion to disqualify Hippler questions his impartiality.

"This motion does not rest upon one adverse ruling, one harsh statement, or the mere fact that the judge who presided over Bryan Kohberger’s criminal case has been assigned to his post-conviction proceeding," the motion states. "It rests upon the extraordinary convergence of all of them."

Although his original criminal trial was relocated to Ada County in 2024 to ensure an impartial jury and adequate resources, his lawyers argue those concerns are irrelevant to a bench proceeding decided solely by a judge.
BRYAN KOHBERGER'S POST-CONVICTION RELIEF BID ENABLED BY FLAWED PLEA DEAL, PSYCHOLOGIST ARGUES

Kohberger, 31, last year pleaded guilty to four counts of first-degree murder and a felony burglary charge for the 2022 stabbing deaths of University of Idaho students Madison Mogen, 21, Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, 20.
However, Kohberger is now asking to be granted a trial even though he could possibly face the death penalty.

The central pillar of the motion to remove the judge rests on the "constitutional adequacy" of the trial counsel's preparation. Defense lawyers argued the capital trial schedule made it impossible to review the massive amount of evidence in the case.
The defense cautioned the court that forcing it to proceed to trial under those conditions threatened Kohberger’s constitutional right to effective representation.
Hippler rejected the defense’s claims that it was unprepared for trial, accusing it of using the massive volume of discovery as a tactic for delay rather than a genuine concern.
KOHBERGER DEFENSE TEAM SAYS IT IS 'APPALLED' BY FORMER EXPERT'S PUBLIC COMMENTS ABOUT IDAHO MURDERS CASE
The motion also refers to Hippler's statement during sentencing in which he made pronouncements regarding Kohberger's ability to tell the truth.
"Do we really believe, after all of this, he is capable of speaking the truth?" he said, according to the document.
The judge also called Kohberger a "faceless coward" and the "the worst of the worst."

"Those statements are fundamentally different from believing Kohberger committed terrible crimes or deserved severe punishment," the motion states. "They are forward-looking judgments about his credibility. And credibility may now be at the center of this proceeding."

"Transfer is warranted in a case like this where ‘the convenience of witnesses and the ends of justice would be promoted by the change,’" that motion states.

title: ICE officer charged in Minneapolis shooting released in Texas after judge declines to intervene
summary: Christian Castro, an ICE officer charged in connection with a shooting in Minnesota, was released from lock up in Texas after a judge declined a temporary restraining order.
story: Fox News correspondent Christina Coleman reports from Dallas on a federal judge blocking attempts by Minnesota to extradite ICE agent Christian Castro from Texas. Greg Abbott investigates whether the officer legally qualifies as a fugitive.
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer who was charged in connection with shooting someone in Minnesota earlier this year was released from lockup in Texas on Thursday.

A judge on Wednesday declined to take action to prevent the man's release and force Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to send the individual back to Minnesota. Minnesota officials have been pushing to have the man held as they fight for his extradition in the Hennepin County case.
The man, Christian Castro, "was released at 6:59 a.m.," Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Trevino told Fox News Digital in an email on Thursday.
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced in May that Castro was "being charged with four counts of assault in the second degree and one count of falsely reporting a crime."
JUDGE CLEARS PATH FOR ICE AGENT ACCUSED IN MINNESOTA SHOOTING CASE TO LEAVE TEXAS JAIL

Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer Christian Castro gets into a car surrounded by news reporters moments after being released from the Carrizalez-Rucker Cameron County Detention Center in Brownsville, Texas on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Michael Gonzalez)

"Mr. Castro fired his service weapon at the front door of a home knowing there were people who had just run inside that presented absolutely no harm to him or anyone else," Moriarty asserted, saying the bullet hit Julio Sosa-Celis in the leg and eventually lodged "in the wall of a child's bedroom."
Castro was arrested in Texas, and Minnesota has been pressing for Texas to extradite him from the Lone Star State.
'POLITICAL STUNT' PROSECUTION OF ICE AGENT FOR 'ROAD RAGE' PROVOKES HEATED DHS RESPONSE
Christian Castro was released from Texas custody on Aug. 27, 2026. (Cameron County Sheriff's Office)

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez, Jr.'s Wednesday order denying a temporary restraining order declared, "In May, the State of Minnesota charged Castro with various crimes based on that incident. By the time these charges arose, however, Castro was no longer in Minnesota, leading a county judge to issue a nationwide warrant for his arrest. When authorities in the State of Texas arrested Castro in late May, Minnesota Governor Tim Walz initiated the process under the Extradition Act of 1793 and the Uniform Criminal Extradition Act to secure Castro’s extradition to Minnesota."

"Under the UCEA, Castro can be detained on the strength of the Minnesota warrant only until August 27, 2026. As the day approached, and fearing that Castro will flee into Mexico should he be released, Minnesota made repeated inquiries of Texas regarding the status of the extradition request. On August 18, having not received a definitive answer, Minnesota filed this action, alleging that Governor Abbott 'has refused' to sign a rendition warrant, violating the Extradition Clause of the United States Constitution, the Extradition Act, and the UCEA," the order stated.
ABBOTT TAUNTS FAR-LEFT AG WITH FIERY WARNING OVER ICE EXTRADITION FIGHT: 'SUCH BAD LAWYERS'
ICE agents depart the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building on Feb. 4, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minn. (John Moore/Getty Images)

story: The climber was stuck on the side of Mount Yonah, a 3,166-foot mountain ridge in the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest in North Georgia.

The climber, who hasn't been identified by authorities, was stuck on the west face of Mount Yonah, a 3,166-foot mountain ridge in the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest in North Georgia.
According to White County Public Safety officials, the man called 911 at around 7 p.m. to report that he was unable to safely climb up or down the mountain.
Authorities used a drone to locate the man, who was standing on a 20" by 20" ledge approximately 260 feet up the mountain.
11 VISITORS TRAPPED AS DANGEROUS FLASH FLOODING TEARS THROUGH ICONIC NATIONAL PARK
White County firefighter Will Roper maneuvers underneath the free climber, who was stranded on Georgia's Mount Yonah on the night of Aug. 25, 2026. (White County Public Safety)

White County firefighter Will Roper rappelled down the mountain to reach the man. Drone video showed Roper maneuvering beneath him before securing him in a harness and clipping him to the rope. The climber was then hoisted to the top of the mountain.
The entire rescue operation took about 42 minutes, officials said.
Roper told FOX 5 Atlanta said this was the first time he's had to rescue someone on a mountain.
Firefighter Will Roper goes over the edge of Mount Yonah on Aug. 25 to rescue a stranded climber. (White County Public Safety)
FIREFIGHTERS, POLICE PULL YOUNG WOMAN FROM SEWAGE-FILLED RAVINE AFTER DAYS TRAPPED IN 104-DEGREE HEAT
"I've done a lot with dummies and a lot with other firefighters in training, but that's the first time that I've ever done it, kind of in the heat of the moment with a live subject," Roper said.
"It was a little nerve-racking going over the edge," he added.
Roper said the climber was strikingly calm, telling FOX 5 he jokingly asked him: "Have you been rescued before? You're pretty good at this."
Will Roper and the free climber are seen on the west face of Mount Yonah during the Aug. 25 rescue operation. (White County Public Safety)

The climber told Roper that he had experience with Mount Yonah but simply picked the wrong route and got stuck.
"I've been on kind of a high since then, just to have the first rescue," Roper said, adding that he was glad to be able to help someone using his technical training.

title: New Hampshire man allegedly steals rescue truck from firefighters battling his burning home
summary: Nestor Roman II of New Hampshire allegedly stole a rescue truck during a fire at his Dalton home, nearly striking three firefighters before crashing miles away.
story: Southlake Police Corporal Joshua Swisher is hailed a hero for saving a driver from a burning car in Texas. Dramatic dashcam video shows Swisher pulling the man to safety moments before the vehicle was engulfed in flames. Swisher recounts his quick actions and training, expressing relief for the positive outcome and the pride his kids feel seeing him on television.

A New Hampshire man whose home was going up in flames allegedly stole a rescue truck from responding firefighters, then crashed into a fire engine, drove over active hoses and narrowly missed three firefighters before fleeing the scene, authorities said.
Nestor Roman II, 30, of Dalton, faces multiple charges after authorities said he stole the rescue vehicle and later crashed several miles from his burning home.

According to New Hampshire State Police, troopers were responding around 3:50 a.m. Tuesday to assist Dalton Fire & Rescue with a house fire when they learned that a Whitefield Fire & Rescue vehicle had been stolen.
NYC 5-ALARM FIRE INJURES AT LEAST 17 FIREFIGHTERS, OTHERS AS BLAZE DAMAGES MULTIPLE APARTMENT BUILDINGS

Firefighters battled a fully involved house fire in Dalton, New Hampshire, before the homeowner allegedly stole a rescue truck and fled the scene, authorities said. (New Hampshire State Police; Whitefield Firefighters Association)
Dalton Fire & Rescue said crews had been dispatched to a fully involved structure fire near Faraway Road and Mountain Road, with several neighboring departments responding as mutual aid.
As firefighters battled the blaze, Roman allegedly got into Whitefield Fire & Rescue's F550 rescue truck and drove away shortly before 5 a.m., according to the fire department.
NY POLICE CAR CATCHES FIRE, TROOPERS INJURED IN 3-CAR COLLISION
Fire officials said the Dalton home was a "complete loss," while the New Hampshire State Fire Marshal's Office is investigating the cause of the blaze. (Dalton Fire & Rescue)
The department said Roman allegedly drove around Whitefield's E3 fire engine, nearly striking two firefighters and narrowly missing a third who could have been pinned between the two large trucks.
Roman then allegedly crashed into the E3 and a small pickup while "forcing their way onto the road ahead," according to the department.
State police said Roman drove over multiple water supply lines while fleeing. Dalton Fire & Rescue said two charged hoses being used to fight the fire were run over but were not damaged.

Roman also allegedly struck a firefighter's personal vehicle farther down the road and damaged neighboring property, according to fire officials. State police said wooden fences at two separate properties were also damaged.
WATCH: MISSOURI SUSPECT DIVES HEADFIRST OFF BRIDGE IN WILD BID TO EVADE DEPUTIES
Nestor Roman II, 30, faces multiple charges after authorities accused him of stealing a rescue truck from firefighters responding to a blaze at his home. (New Hampshire State Police)
The escape came to an end several miles away after a Dalton homeowner reported that the stolen rescue vehicle had crashed on their property, according to state police.
The homeowner also reported that Roman was allegedly attempting to take items from the porch.
Troopers arrived moments later and found Roman on the porch. Police said he was uncooperative but was ultimately taken into custody.
Roman was charged with three felony counts of reckless conduct with a deadly weapon, burglary and two counts of theft by unauthorized taking.

He also faces misdemeanor charges of obstructing government administration, four counts of conduct after an accident, resisting arrest and detention, driving after suspension subsequent and two counts of driving over a fire hose without consent, according to state police.
Despite sustaining significant damage, Whitefield's E3 was able to remain in operation, and firefighters ultimately extinguished the flames.
MYSTERY STRANGER VANISHES AFTER FAMILY SAYS FRANTIC WARNING SAVED THEIR LIVES DURING DEVASTATING HOUSE FIRE
Multiple fire departments responded to a house fire in Dalton, New Hampshire, that took a chaotic turn when the homeowner allegedly stole a rescue vehicle. (Dalton Fire & Rescue)
Fire officials said the house was a "complete loss."
The New Hampshire State Fire Marshal's Office is investigating the cause of the fire.

"We are extremely thankful that no firefighters were physically injured despite the close call," Dalton Fire & Rescue said in a statement.

title: Fiery views on Lindsay Clancy at work could get you fired — and be perfectly legal, employment lawyer warns
summary: Lindsay Clancy's murder trial has sparked heated workplace debates, but an employment law expert warns fiery opinions could legally get you fired.
story: New York lawyer Nicole Brenecki warns that arguing over the Lindsay Clancy case in most workplaces is not protected speech — and could even get you fired.

Sharing fiery views at work about the Massachusetts mom accused of killing her three young children could get you canned and still be legal, according to an expert on employment law who is following the case.

Lindsay Clancy, 36, is accused of strangling her children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — and trying to end her own life by dropping from a second-floor window after sending her husband to pick up takeout and something from a pharmacy, according to the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office.

The case has drawn national attention, pro-Clancy protesters to the courthouse and impassioned discussions about who is responsible online after her defense argued she is not guilty by reason of insanity or mental defect.

"That disciplinary measure, it's not on its face illegal if you get fired for starting, you know, fiery speech about Lindsay Clancy and how you support her," said Nicole Brenecki, a New York-based attorney who specializes in employment law.
LINDSAY CLANCY MURDER TRIAL BECOMES SOCIAL MEDIA OBSESSION AS TIKTOKERS, SLEUTHS DEBATE CONTROVERSIAL CASE

Lindsay Clancy is wheeled into Plymouth Superior Court on Friday, Feb. 20, 2026. Clancy became paraplegic when she harmed herself and jumped out of a second-story window at her home after the deaths of her three children. She is charged with murder in the children's deaths. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)
Still, Brenecki warned, a fired employee could still raise legal concerns if their Clancy-related statements were used as a pretext to get rid of them for other reasons.
"If a case like this came to the court system, it would not be viewed in the context of the free speech alone," she said. "It would also be viewed in the contexts of employment laws."
Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside of Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 20, 2026. (John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)
LINDSAY CLANCY TRIAL: POSTPARTUM IS REAL, BUT CHILD KILLING DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY, VETERAN PROSECUTOR SAYS
As a "general rule," however, she said employers would be allowed to prohibit such discussions about the case.

Other considerations would involve whether the speech took place during working hours, disrupted business operations or whether there was discrimination against protected groups involved in the firing.
Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

"Every single case in our court system is very highly and intensely fact-based," she said. "So we cannot give...any specific explanation as to whether something would be illegal or not. We have to look at the facts."

Still, Brenecki advised against arguing over strong opinions at the water cooler.

Supporters of Lindsay Clancy's pose for a photo outside of Plymouth Superior Court, Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Clancy is on trial for the murder of her three children in January 2023. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

"If you truly want to voice them in a workplace, then be prepared to have to find greener pastures," she said.

There could be other consequences as well. Earlier this month, an attorney named Alex Thomason said in a TikTok video of his own that he has already spoken with men involved in custody disputes with women who have been posting the "solidarity hold a heart thing" for Clancy.
In one instance, he said, he is looking to have a woman's visitation rights stripped away.
"I want to be able to have a forensic psychiatrist interview this woman just to see how wack-a-doodle she is, and we're gonna use her TikTok posts," he said.

Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside of Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 20, 2026. (John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has argued that Clancy was under the effects of postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors allege she acted deliberately and understood what she was doing was wrong.

A Lindsay Clancy supporters dressed in pink outside Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth. Mass., Monday, Aug. 24, 20206. Clancy's murder trial is in its final stages.  (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

LINDSAY CLANCY DIDN'T SHOW 'BREAK WITH REALITY' AS JURY WEIGHS PSYCHOSIS DEFENSE: SUSAN SMITH PROSECUTOR
Jurors began deliberating after both sides delivered their closing arguments Thursday.

title: Suspected human smugglers lead cops on 100-mph chase before bailing and allegedly committing armed carjacking
summary: Helicopter video captures the 100-mph chase in Fabens, Texas, as two suspected human smugglers bail out and one allegedly carjacks a civilian at gunpoint.
story: Aerial video shows authorities pursuing suspected human smugglers in Texas before the vehicle was disabled and the occupants fled, with officials saying one suspect later carjacked a civilian at gunpoint. (@CBPCommissioner via X)
Two suspected human smugglers led authorities on a 100-mph chase in Texas on Thursday before bailing out of their vehicle, with one allegedly carjacking a civilian at gunpoint, authorities said.
Helicopter video from U.S. Customs and Border Protection's Air and Marine Operations shows the high-speed pursuit unfolding along Interstate 10 in Fabens.
Authorities are seen pursuing the suspected human smugglers before their vehicle was disabled and both occupants fled on foot.
VIDEO SHOWS ILLEGAL ALIENS FOUND CRAMMED INSIDE SEMI-TRUCK SLEEPER CAB IN ALLEGED SMUGGLING BUST
Two suspected human smugglers bailed out of their vehicle after a high-speed pursuit in Texas, authorities said. (CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott via X)
An official can be heard over radio communications saying the vehicle's front right tire may have been damaged by a spike strip.
Moments later, the vehicle slows down and two occupants jump out and run.
"Bail out, bail out, bail out!" someone is heard shouting in the video.
The two men are then seen running across the highway, with one quickly apprehended by a member of the Texas Department of Public Safety.
2 COLOMBIAN NATIONALS ARRESTED IN STOLEN MERCEDES LINKED TO VIOLENT CALIFORNIA CARJACKING
Helicopter video shows authorities pursuing suspected human smugglers during a high-speed chase along Interstate 10 in Fabens, Texas. (CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott via X.)
The other suspect allegedly carjacked a civilian at gunpoint before he was also later taken into custody, authorities said.
Authorities have not released information about how many people were allegedly being smuggled or their nationalities.
"Outstanding coordination by Border Patrol, AMO, HSI and Texas DPS," CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott posted on X alongside video of the pursuit.

"Suspected human smugglers hit 100+ mph and bailed out when their vehicle was disabled," Scott continued. "One then carjacked a civilian at gunpoint. Smugglers risk lives for profit. We will keep taking them down."

title: California authorities identify final unknown victim of ‘Happy Face Killer’ Keith Jesperson after 34 years
summary: DNA testing confirmed Lydia Jane Wade McWhorter as the 'Happy Face Killer's' final unidentified victim, found along a California highway in 1992.
story: California investigators reveal how DNA testing helped solve a decades-old mystery surrounding one of serial killer Keith Hunter Jesperson’s victims, now identified as Lydia Jane Wade McWhorter of Texas. (Credit: X @ Riverside County DA's Office)

The final unidentified victim of notorious serial killer Keith Hunter Jesperson, known as the "Happy Face Killer," has been identified more than three decades after her body was discovered along a California highway, authorities announced Thursday.

The Riverside County District Attorney's Office identified the woman, long known to investigators only as "Claudia," as Lydia Jane Wade McWhorter of Texas, after DNA testing confirmed a connection to a member of her maternal family.
McWhorter's body was discovered Aug. 30, 1992, along Highway 95 about seven miles north of Blythe, California.
Jesperson, a long-haul truck driver who confessed to killing eight women across multiple states, later admitted killing her.
Jesperson told investigators he knew the woman as "Claudia," but authorities were unable to determine whether that was her real name.
INVESTIGATORS FIND RELATIVES OF ‘HAPPY FACE’ SERIAL KILLER’S LAST UNKNOWN VICTIM IN MISSION TO IDENTIFY HER

Keith Hunter Jesperson, center, listens as Don Findlay, far right, son of murder victim Julie Ann Winningham, addresses the court during sentencing on Dec. 19, 1995, at the Clark County Courthouse, in Vancouver, Wash. (Jeremiah Coughlan/AP Photo/The Columbian, File)

The identification comes after Riverside County investigators publicly renewed their effort to identify McWhorter in 2024, when genetic genealogy had connected the unknown victim to relatives on her father's side but had not produced the maternal connection needed to confirm her identity.

Fox News Digital reported at the time that DNA testing had identified Summer Gonzales as the victim's paternal half-sister. Gonzales said she wanted to learn her sister's real name and eventually lay her to rest with family.

An investigative lead ultimately brought the cold case team to one of McWhorter's direct maternal relatives, according to the district attorney's office. Investigators then identified a possible genetic connection to another member of the maternal family.
A DNA sample confirmed that connection earlier this week, allowing investigators to positively identify McWhorter nearly 34 years after her body was found, authorities said.
REMAINS FOUND IN UTAH DESERT 28 YEARS AGO WITH HELP OF A PSYCHIC FINALLY IDENTIFIED THROUGH DNA GENEALOGY
Lydia Jane Wade McWhorter, whose body was found near Blythe, Calif., in 1992, was identified nearly 34 years later through DNA testing. (Riverside County District Attorney's Office)
McWhorter's sisters, who grew up with her, had spent decades without knowing what happened to her after she disappeared from Texas in the 1990s, according to prosecutors.

"I want to thank the public for the role you play in our investigations," Billy Hester, supervising investigator of the Cold Case Unit, said in a news release. "When people take the time to share information, submit a tip or simply pay attention to what is happening in their community, it can make a real difference. You may not know where a piece of information will lead, but our investigators will follow it. Most importantly, I hope this will finally bring closure to Lydia’s family."
The district attorney's Division of Victim Services is working with McWhorter's family as they decide how to honor her and lay her to rest.
'HAPPY FACE' KILLER WARNS FELLOW SERIAL KILLER REX HEUERMANN COULD BE 'TOSSED TO THE WOLVES' IN PRISON
Lydia Jane Wade McWhorter disappeared from Texas in the 1990s before her body was found along Highway 95 near Blythe, Calif., in August 1992. (Riverside County District Attorney's Office)
Jesperson was arrested in 1995, and eventually confessed to killing eight women between 1990 and 1995 in California, Washington state, Oregon, Florida, Nebraska and Wyoming.
He became known as the "Happy Face Killer" after sending letters about his crimes to the media that he signed with a smiley face.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
He pleaded guilty to McWhorter's murder in Riverside County on Jan. 8, 2010, and was sentenced to 25 years to life in prison.
He is serving multiple life sentences in Oregon.
With McWhorter's identification, Riverside County's cold case team has now closed the final unidentified-victim case tied to the murders for which Jesperson was convicted.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Maine meteorologist suffers giggle attack on live TV after prank backfires spectacularly
summary: Patrick Osborn struggled to finish his WABI weather report after a prank involving Charlie Brown audio sent him into a fit of laughter.
story: WABI Meteorologist Patrick Osborn said an attempt to prank a coworker backfired spectacularly while he was attempting to deliver a live forecast (Credit: WABI).

A local meteorologist is experiencing viral fame after he was caught on live television suddenly breaking into an uncontrollable fit of giggles that grew increasingly hysterical as he struggled to keep his composure.

Patrick Osborn, who was delivering a regularly scheduled weather report on Maine news station WABI, left viewers completely stunned Sunday morning as he repeatedly tried, and failed, to hold back his laughter.
In the video, Osborn was seen gasping for breath as he blurted out temperatures between chuckles, repeatedly apologizing before the laughter finally rendered his speech completely incomprehensible.
The laughing fit stretched on for about a minute, with Osborn stepping off camera before returning and eventually tossing back to a colleague.
SPORTS COMMENTATOR MICHAEL HOLLEY IS 'FINE' AFTER FAINTING DURING LIVE BROADCAST IN TERRIFYING SCENE
The meteorologist was unable to control his laughter. His on-air giggle fit has now gone viral.  (WABI)

Recalling the moment with WABI co-anchor Brian Sullivan, Osborn said, "I got a fit of laughter that I was not able to control on air, unfortunately. A lot of times, something funny happens, and I’m able to contain myself, but this one, it was just a little too overwhelming."
He revealed that the laughter was triggered by a prank he had attempted to play on fellow anchor Josh Gabbard, only for the joke to backfire on him.

During a commercial break, Osborn said he played a short Charlie Brown video for its sound effects but failed to realize the clip was actually an hour-long compilation that periodically replayed the sound every few minutes.
DAD JOKES MAY BE GOOD FOR YOUR BRAIN IN ONE SURPRISING WAY, EXPERTS SAY
Viral video shows WABI meteorologist Patrick Osborn struggling through a Maine weather report amid an uncontrollable laughter fit. (WABI)
He said the audio then unexpectedly played again while he was starting his weather segment, almost instantly sending him into hysterical laughter.

"It’s the Charlie Brown phone call noise. It’s one where his mom or teacher calls him, and it’s the ‘Wa, wa, wa,’" Osborn told his station. "Something as silly and light-hearted as a Charlie Brown sound made me completely lose my composure."

"I was just trying to keep it together but I couldn't. Like, when you're not supposed to laugh, you're in an environment when you can't laugh, and you're trying to hold it back, that just makes it 10 times worse," he said.
Osborn added: "I tried to get through it," but "Josh had to leave the studio."
The WABI meteorologist tried to prank a fellow anchor during a break, but the joke spilled into his weather segment and backfired. (WABI)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Thats the hardest I’ve heard … really anyone laugh," Sullivan said, laughing along.WABI posted the clip to TikTok. As of Thursday night, the clip had nearly nine million views.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Teens accused of destroying Flock camera until battery exploded, igniting fire near homes: report
summary: Three South Carolina teens allegedly cut down a Flock Safety camera pole and hammered its battery until it exploded, causing over $5,000 in damage.
story: Flock Safety CEO Garrett Langley defended his company's automated license plate reading cameras on 'Fox & Friends.' As critics raise privacy concerns over the cameras tracking vehicles, Langley noted that the technology helped solve more than 1 million crimes last year.

Three South Carolina teenagers were arrested after allegedly cutting down a Flock Safety camera pole and beating its battery pack with a hammer until it exploded and burst into flames, authorities said.
The attack unfolded during the early morning hours of Aug. 15 along Harmony Church Road in the Edgemoor area of Chester County, according to WBTV, citing the Chester County Sheriff’s Office.

Investigators said the teens hacked down the pole before striking the equipment with a hammer, setting off the battery fire. The sheriff’s office estimated the damage at more than $5,000, WBTV reported.

Blaze Fuller, Samuel Carlisle and James Ryerson, all 19, were arrested and charged with criminal conspiracy and malicious injury to personal property, according to jail records reviewed by Fox News Digital.

Fuller was booked Aug. 18 and released the following day after posting $5,000 bond. Carlisle and Ryerson were also booked Aug. 18 and released Aug. 19, records show.
The blaze left a nearby resident worried it could have turned into something far worse.
"My house is over here," Edgemoor resident David Cunupp told WBTV, pointing toward his property. "Could’ve caught fire and burned if it wasn’t for the rain."
Cunupp said he was not necessarily opposed to the cameras but questioned the role of a private company in running the surveillance technology.
"They could be used for good, but I don’t see where a private company’s got access or running it instead of the DMV or the government," Cunupp told the outlet.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Chester County Sheriff’s Office for comment.

The alleged fiery takedown comes as tensions over Flock’s automated license plate reader network mount nationwide, with privacy advocates, local officials and lawmakers challenging the spread of vehicle location databases.
HAWLEY RIPS FLOCK’S SPRAWLING SURVEILLANCE WEB AS TEXAS CITIES CUT CAMERAS OVER PRIVACY AND DATA FEARS
An aerial view shows a Flock Safety camera mounted on a light pole in Burbank, Calif., on Aug. 3, 2026. (Getty Images)
Opponents of the cameras have condemned vandalism and instead called for the technology to be challenged through lawful action.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., chairman of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, launched an investigation into Flock this week, saying the company has built an "unprecedented national surveillance network" with more than 120,000 cameras across 49 states and more than 20 billion vehicle scans each month.
POWERFUL CRIME-FIGHTING SURVEILLANCE GROWTH SPURS LAWMAKERS TO ISSUE WARNING: 'ORWELLIAN'
A Flock Safety camera is mounted to a light pole Aug. 3, 2026, in Beverly Hills, Calif. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

"Instead of serving discrete local investigations, as contemplated by our constitutional processes and safeguards, these camera networks harness artificial intelligence to pool what they capture into a national database that customers can search," Hawley wrote in a letter to Flock CEO Garrett Langley.

Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel previously told Fox News Digital the company would respond directly to Hawley’s questions and looked forward to explaining "the safeguards built into our platform and how law enforcement agencies use Flock to solve crime and find missing people."
FLOCK SURVEILLANCE SPREADS ACROSS THE SOUTH AS RED STATE LAWMAKERS SEEK TO AX '1984'-STYLE TRACKING TOOLS
Protesters rally against the use of Flock cameras April 3, 2026, outside City Hall in Troy, N.Y. (Jim Franco/Times Union via Getty Images)

The dispute has played out through local government action in Texas. Hood County officials voted to end their relationship with Flock and later directed that the county’s three cameras be disconnected and covered until they could be removed.
Constable John Shirley shared photos of the covered cameras in a Facebook post, calling it "a good day for the Freedom of the people of Hood County."
He said the cameras had been "constantly scanning and recording regular folks just going about their day."
REPS ANDY HARRIS, KEITH SELF, SEN RICK SCOTT: FIX FISA. DON’T SPY ON US
FILE - Officials in Hood County, Texas, cover a Flock automated license plate reader camera after the county ended its relationship with the company. (Hood County Constable, Precinct 2 Facebook)
"That kind of permanent, warrantless tracking doesn’t belong in a free society," Shirley wrote. "Privacy isn’t optional, and mass surveillance isn’t how we do things here."

In a later Facebook post, Shirley said he supports technology that helps police solve crimes, locate missing people and find dangerous suspects but argued public safety cannot end the conversation about individual liberty.
"We can have good policing and still insist on boundaries," Shirley wrote. "We can use technology without giving government unlimited surveillance capability."

The debate has already pushed communities from Texas, Arizona and nationwide, to reconsider or end their Flock contracts, citing worries about data sharing, privacy and misuse.

title: California pastor charged with yearslong child molestation as investigators seek more victims: DA
summary: David Johnson, an Ojai pastor and massage therapist, faces six felony child molestation charges in Ventura County as investigators seek more victims.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A California pastor and massage therapist has pleaded not guilty to charges accusing him of molesting two children under the age of 14 over several years, prosecutors said.
David Johnson, 58, of Ojai, faces six felony child molestation charges in Ventura County, according to the Ventura County District Attorney’s Office.
Investigators are also looking for possible additional victims and have publicly asked anyone with information about Johnson or other possible unreported crimes to come forward.
Johnson is accused of molesting two children who were under 14 years old at the time of the alleged abuse.
Prosecutors said the alleged abuse occurred over several years at locations in Ojai and Oxnard.
SAN FRANCISCO ARCHDIOCESE AGREES TO $395M SETTLEMENT WITH 530 CLERGY ABUSE SURVIVORS
David Johnson, 58, of Ojai, Calif., faces six felony child molestation charges involving two children under 14. (Ventura County Sheriff's Office)
Johnson, who worked as both a pastor and massage therapist, had access to the children through a familial relationship, according to prosecutors.
Authorities have not publicly identified the children.
Johnson faces four felony counts of committing a lewd act upon a child and two felony counts of continuous sexual abuse.
Prosecutors have also filed special allegations involving substantial sexual conduct and the victims being under 14 years old, according to the district attorney’s office.
EX-TEXAS MIDDLE SCHOOL TEACHER SENTENCED TO 33 YEARS FOR SEXUALLY ABUSING 13-YEAR-OLD STUDENT
The Ventura County District Attorney’s Office has charged Johnson with six felony child molestation charges. (Ventura County District Attorney's Office/Facebook)
Johnson was arrested Monday on charges of child molestation by the Ventura County Sheriff’s Office, according to sheriff’s inmate records.
The records show Johnson was arrested shortly before 3 p.m. and booked into the Ventura County Main Jail later that evening.
Johnson appeared in Ventura County Superior Court for his arraignment and pleaded not guilty to all six charges.
He remains in custody without bail and is scheduled to return to Ventura County Superior Court on Friday for a bail review hearing.

title: Former Gitmo prosecutor likens 9/11 trial delay to 'Frankenstein's zombie court'
summary: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and three alleged 9/11 co-conspirators will face trial in June 2028 as the Guantánamo military commission sets new deadlines.
story: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the head plotter, will finally go to trial years after the terror attack.

Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the Sept. 11 terror attacks, and three alleged co-conspirators will finally stand trial in 2028, as the case against them has languished amid lengthy delays and a protracted process that one expert has likened to "Frankenstein's zombie court."

A military judge on Wednesday set the long-delayed trial for June 5, 2028, while establishing deadlines for the case. Much to the frustration of the loved ones of those who died during the attacks, Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators have been held at a military detention center in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, for more than two decades.
The problem, according to Michael Lebowitz, a former Guantánamo military commissions prosecutor, isn't the evidence against the terror suspects — it's the system.
NEW EVIDENCE IN LOCKERBIE PAN AM FLIGHT 103 BOMBING CASE PUSHES FEDERAL JUDGE TO POSTPONE TRIAL

Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks, has been held at Guantánamo Bay since 2003. Mohammed and three of his alleged co-conspirators are expected to stand trial in June 2028, nearly three decades after the terror attacks. (Getty Images)

"It's the system and how it evolved and was created. And it's also an issue of Guantánamo Bay itself, where Gitmo is an adequate, albeit expensive, option for things like detaining suspected war criminals and even migrants," Lebowitz told Fox News Digital.

"The problem is that we used to call it the traveling circus because, in order to even conduct the smallest court hearing, everybody has to go to Washington, D.C., and get on an airplane," he continued. "I'm talking judges. I'm talking prosecutors, defense counsel, witnesses and court people."
TRUMP TURNS TO 'ZOMBIE' COURT AFTER BOASBERG POINTED TO IT IN DEPORTATION FIGHT

The case of Mohammed, as well as Walid bin Attash, Mustafa al-Hawsawi and Ammar al-Baluchi, has been delayed for decades amid lengthy legal wrangling, including failed efforts to resolve the case through plea agreements.

The 2028 date sets a timetable for a case that has remained in pretrial proceedings for years as the military commission has addressed disputes over evidence and other legal issues before a trial on the merits can begin, Fox News Digital previously reported.
NEW 9/11 MUSEUM EXHIBIT AIMS TO CONNECT YOUNGER AMERICANS TO THE ATTACKS THROUGH POWERFUL ARTIFACTS

This Jan. 21, 2009 sketch reviewed by the U.S. military, shows, from top left, Khalid Shaikh Mohammad; Walid bin Attash; Ramzi bin al Shibh; Ali Abdul Aziz Ali, also known as Ammar al Baluchi, and Mustafa al Hawsawi attend a hearing at the U.S. Military Commissions court for war crimes at the U.S. Naval Base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.  (AP Photo/Janet Hamlin, Pool)

Mohammed, a Pakistani citizen, is accused of masterminding the attacks in which hijackers crashed commercial airliners into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon. A fourth hijacked plane, United Airlines Flight 93, crashed in Pennsylvania after passengers attempted to overtake the hijackers.

The case has had more than 10 judges, Lebowitz said, meaning lawyers have had to keep relitigating the same "mundane" issues. Lebowitz, an Army veteran, participated in a number of cases in Guantanamo, including the 9/11 case and the bombing of the USS Cole.
TRUMP ADMIN INVOKES 30-YEAR DORMANT TERROR COURT AS IT SEEKS TO DEPORT AFGHAN WOMAN TIED TO ELECTION DAY PLOT

"What I found was that the way the system has kind of been set up and how it evolved and turned into, it's essentially a candy store for defense lawyers, where the judges don't have teeth to control the courtroom like you would in federal court," he said. "It just goes from there where defense lawyers can really grease up the system and grease up the gears and really grind it to a halt."

One issue prosecutors will have to iron out is whether to seek the death penalty, Lebowitz said. Even if Mohammed and the other suspected terrorists are condemned to death, it's highly unlikely to be upheld, he said.
I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES
Two flags flutter on a fence in front of lower Manhattan and One World Trade Center at the Tear Drop 9/11 Memorial at sunset on June 13, 2026, in Bayonne, New Jersey. (Gary Hershorn/Getty Images)
"You're dealing with cases where, essentially, the defense lawyers would put the CIA on trial for their treatment of detainees after 9/11," he noted.
Despite some of the suspected 9/11 suspects finally getting their day in court, families of the victims also want Saudi Arabia to be held responsible.

"I think we’d ask the same question about the case against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, whose agents supported al-Qaeda and the terrorist hijackers, too, after they arrived in the U.S., Terry Strada, national chair of 9/11 Families United, told Fox News Digital.

In 2024, Mohammed, bin Attash and al-Hawsawi agreed to admit their roles in the terror attacks in exchange for serving life sentences and avoiding the death penalty. While some 9/11 families supported the idea, others blasted the deal.
Amid the criticism, the Biden administration withdrew the plea deal, resulting in more litigation.
Fox News Digital's Brittany Miller contributed to this report.
