Cuba, Iran and North Korea remain the three countries designated by Washington as state sponsors of terrorism.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Putin ‘panicked’ as defiant Ukraine marks Independence Day under Russian bombardment
summary: Ukraine celebrated 35 years of independence amid fresh Russian attacks as an expert said Kyiv’s deep strikes and battlefield pressure have left Putin rattled.
story: Ukraine's Independence Day faced heightened security risks as former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Carrie Filipetti, now executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, says Vladimir Putin is "panicked."

Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day on Monday under the shadow of continued Russian attacks, with one regional security expert arguing that Russian President Vladimir Putin is "panicked" as Ukrainian forces strike deeper inside Russia.

The anniversary, commemorating Ukraine's Aug. 24, 1991, declaration of independence from the Soviet Union, came amid intensified Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure and heightened security concerns after Ukraine's Security Service warned of possible terrorist attacks ahead of the holiday.

European leaders joined Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv for Independence Day events in a show of support as the war grinds on. Zelenskyy declared that Ukraine wants peace but is not prepared to surrender to Moscow's demands.
A Russian drone strike Friday on a packed shopping center in Kryvyi Rih, Zelenskyy’s hometown, killed at least 16 people and injured 130, according to The Associated Press.
'PURE HELL' IN MOSCOW AS UKRAINIAN DRONES STRIKE MAJOR REFINERY SUPPLYING CAPITAL'S FUEL MARKET

FILE - Russian President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting aboard the missile cruiser Varyag in Russia's far eastern Sakhalin region on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Putin previously said Russia is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe. (Reuters)
Putin has warned that Ukrainian strikes on Russian economic targets open a "Pandora’s box," while Kyiv maintains deep strikes are vital to disrupting Moscow’s logistics.
Ukraine has targeted Russian economic infrastructure, including warehouses belonging to online retailers Wildberries and Ozon.

"The war with Russia has seen a lot of advances for the Ukrainians over this year," former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Carrie Filipetti, now executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, told Fox News Digital.
"They've recently been able to actually penetrate much deeper into Russian territory, including close to Moscow and St. Petersburg."

"Their success on the military front has now resulted in the Russians getting panicked and starting to attack more inside Ukraine and what they're really trying to do is weaken their will and capabilities," Filipetti said, adding that Putin "gets very anxious when he's put in a corner."

"What we're seeing is these sorts of gasps at trying to retain some kind of control," Filipetti added. "This is why he recently targeted a shopping mall inside Ukrainian territory. He is not focused on targeting military assets. He is really focused on trying to defeat the will of Ukrainians by attacking them."
RUSSIA UNLEASHES NEARLY 600 MISSILES AND DRONES ON KYIV IN DEADLIEST STRIKE SINCE MAY
The anniversary came amid intensified Russian strikes. (REUTERS /Gleb Garanich)
Filipetti warned the targeting of civilian areas created heightened security risks as Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day, more than four years into Russia's full-scale invasion.

Several European leaders traveled to Kyiv for Ukraine’s Independence Day events, including European Council President António Costa and leaders from Finland, Lithuania, Norway, Denmark, Estonia and Latvia.
Filipetti said the high-level participation underscored continued international support for Ukraine.
TRUMP'S TURKEY ARMS SALE PROPOSAL SPARKS CONGRESSIONAL QUESTIONS BEFORE NATO SUMMIT

Ukrainian authorities urged citizens to stay vigilant on public transport and guard against potential sabotage or sharing media that could reveal military positions, as well as possible attacks, Ukrainian News reported. (HENRY NICHOLLS / Pool via REUTERS)

"Independence Day is a really important moment for the allies of the Ukrainians to really show that we are not losing steam, that we continue to support their operations, to continue to support their sovereignty," Filipetti said. "But anytime there's massive public gatherings, particularly to demonstrate patriotism and support for the Ukrainian state, it increases the security risk."

Ukrainian authorities urged citizens to stay vigilant on public transport and guard against potential sabotage or sharing media that could reveal military positions, as well as possible attacks, Ukrainian News reported.
"They should be particularly mindful about sharing any videos or photographs that could betray the locations of some of their frontline soldiers," Filipetti warned.
DRONE OFFENSIVE HITS RUSSIAN OIL TANKERS AND REFINERIES AT 'INDUSTRIAL SCALE' AS MOSCOW BANS DIESEL EXPORTS

Russian glide bombs strike food processing plant in Zaporizhzhia Rescuers work at the site of a reported strike on a food processing plant in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on July 8, 2026.  (Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Monday's holiday came after a lethal exchange of drone and missile strikes. Ukrainian officials reported at least seven deaths from Russian attacks, while a Ukrainian drone strike in Russia's Krasnodar region killed three, according to Russian officials, The Associated Press reported.

"The Russians really want to bleed the Ukrainians of people, equipment, and will before the Russians are bled of those same three things," Filipetti said. "And what we've seen over the course of this year is almost no territorial gains on behalf of the Russians."
They are losing more soldiers each month than they can recruit, forcing them to rely on North Korean, Cuban and other foreign fighters to fill the gap, Filipetti added.
ZELENSKYY SAYS PUTIN 'LOST THE INITIATIVE' AS UKRAINE'S TECH INDUSTRY RESHAPES THE WAR

President Vladimir Putin prioritizes Russia's nuclear triad strengthening as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns the Russian leader has launched "World War III." (Genya SAVILOV / AFP via Getty ImagesContributor / Getty Images)
"Remember, Putin thought that this was going to be a special military operation that was going to last a matter of weeks," Filipetti said.
Ultimately, she emphasized that Ukraine's resolve delivers a firm deterrent beyond Moscow.

"It sends a message to the Russians that any invasion of sovereign territory, like their invasion of Ukraine, is going to create more consequences for them," Filipetti said. "We are not losing steam, and we continue to support their operations, to continue to support their sovereignty."
Filipetti said it also sends an important message to other American adversaries like China.

"These adversaries of the United States really learned from how the United States handles conflicts in other theaters. It's really important that our adversaries of China, Russia, Iran, and others understand that if they invade another country unilaterally, there are going to be consequences, not rewards."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Iran tried to assassinate one of Netanyahu's sons, prime minister says
summary: Benjamin Netanyahu claims Iran tried to murder one of his sons, urging enhanced protection for prime ministerial candidates during the election campaign.
story: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warns Iran of a forceful response to any future attacks, emphasizing Israel's right to self-defense after recent clashes. The segment explores the volatile Middle East situation, including Iran's use of Hezbollah and the US administration's role in fostering regional alliances. Internal protests against the Iranian government are also discussed.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Iran of attempting to assassinate one of his sons on Monday.
Netanyahu made the accusation during an interview with Israel's Channel 14, saying he has asked Israeli law enforcement to boost protection measures for any prime ministerial candidate.
"This is an unbelievable case. Iran targeted one of my sons. Iran tried to murder him, tried to murder one of my sons," Netanyahu told the station, as reported by the Jerusalem Post.
ISRAEL SHARES INTELLIGENCE WARNING IRAN PLOTTED NEW ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT AGAINST TRUMP: REPORT
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the Shin Bet Special Operations Command Center on Sept. 9, 2025. (Shin Bet Communications)
"Is this part of the intelligence provided to you?" a Channel 14 reporter asked.

"Iran tried to murder one of my sons. And this is why this promise [I am making] is more than a luxury – without it, they could succeed [in killing my son]. People need to show some restraint, especially during an election campaign," Netanyahu said.
ISRAELI POLICE SAY IRAN USING WHATSAPP, FACEBOOK, BLACKMAIL TO RECRUIT SPIES AS LATEST ATTEMPT FOILED
Netanyahu did not clarify which of his two sons was the target of the plot.

Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to members of the media following a meeting with House Speaker Mike Johnson at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on July 8, 2025. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The Israeli security agency Shin Bet granted extended protection services to Netanyahu's wife, Sara, and their sons, Yair and Avner, beginning in July.
ISRAEL FORTIFIES BORDER WITH JORDAN AS IRAN SEEKS NEW TERROR PATH
The prime minister did not describe details of the assassination plot nor did he say how Israeli intelligence became aware of it.
The accusation comes as Israel remains in negotiations for a withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon, where they had been fighting the Iran-backed Hezbollah terrorist group.
LEBANON ACCUSES IRAN OF INSERTING IRGC TERRORISTS INTO COUNTRY 'UNDER GUISE OF DIPLOMATIC ACTIVITY'

The news comes after Israel publicized a massive store of rockets, grenades, drones, sniper rifles, automated weapons, anti-tank rocket launchers, mortars and other military firepower it has confiscated from Hezbollah and Hamas in recent months.

Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi, second from left, commander of the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, attends a conference in Tehran, Iran, on July 4, 2026. (Iranian Presidency/Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The seized weapons, ranging in manufacturers from the Islamic Republic of Iran to Russia and China to homegrown producers in Lebanon and Gaza, and even a Nazi-era gun, were part of the war machinery used by Hamas and Hezbollah against Israeli civilians and the IDF since Hamas terrorists attacked southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
IRAN'S WAR ON AMERICANS BEGAN DECADES AGO. THESE FAMILIES STILL CARRY THE SCARS
Hezbollah and Hamas, known proxies of Iran, have killed over 300 American citizens, according to reports.

The Jewish state fought a multifront war against Iran and its proxies at the height of the conflict. The remains of Iranian rockets litter the ground outside the weapons storage facility at Tzrifin for journalists to inspect.

title: Massive garbage heap collapses onto homes, killing at least 30 as rescuers search for survivors
summary: A mountain of garbage collapsed after heavy rain at a major landfill site in Conakry, Guinea, burying nearby homes and launching a search for survivors.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
At least 30 people were killed in a massive landslide in Guinea on Sunday when a mountainous open-air landfill collapsed and buried nearby shacks, trapping numerous victims beneath a mass of garbage.
The incident happened at Dar Es Salam, the largest waste dump in the West African country's capital, Conakry, according to a report from The Associated Press (AP).
Guinea News reported that the weight of the waste caused a three-story building beneath it to cave in.
Authorities said heavy rainfall also washed over the refuse overnight, creating hazardous conditions at the landfill, according to the AP.
EARTHQUAKE SHAKES PERU'S ANDES REGION, KILLING AT LEAST 5, DISPLACING HUNDREDS
Residents and rescuers use an excavator to search for victims after a landslide struck the Dar Es Salam dumpsite in Conakry, Guinea, on Aug. 23, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
Six people were seriously injured and several homes were destroyed in the incident, according to reports. Officials launched a search-and-rescue operation to find any survivors.

The AP reported that the landfill was originally scheduled to close Sunday after officials warned of hazardous conditions, citing Lt. Col. Baldé Mamadou Bailo, the sanitation officer for the military engineering battalion.
The decision followed reports of a similar incident at the landfill in recent years, raising concerns about its safety.
Thirty people were killed and six others seriously injured after a landslide struck the Dar Es Salam dumpsite in Conakry, Guinea, on Aug. 23, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
As a precautionary measure, residents who lived near the site had also been given eviction notices and were forced to vacate the area, the AP said.
However, many people remained nearby at the time of the disaster, according to reports.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Dar Es Salam landfill collapsed following heavy overnight rain in Conakry, Guinea, on Aug. 23, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
"We will ensure that the remaining families are relocated elsewhere," Dienabou Touré, the minister of territorial administration and decentralization, said at the scene, according to the AP.
Reuters reported that the landfill suffered a similar incident in 2017, when torrential rains caused a mudslide that killed at least eight people.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Mexican governor facing US drug charges seeks leave just one day after returning to office
summary: Embattled Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya's abrupt reversal follows pointed remarks from Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum about putting nation above personal interest.
story: Mexican Senator Lilly Tellez discusses the indictment of a Sinaloa governor and nine officials for alleged fentanyl trafficking. She blasts President Claudia Sheinbaum's refusal to extradite, asserting Mexico operates as a 'narco-state.' Tellez warns of deep corruption and the dire implications for bilateral relations and border security.

Embattled Sinaloa, Mexico, Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya abruptly requested an indefinite leave of absence Saturday, just one day after returning to office following a three-month absence triggered by U.S. drug trafficking charges against him.
Rocha, 77, shared a letter on social media asking for "temporary leave of an indefinite nature, for more than 30 days" from his position as governor.
The letter, dated Aug. 22 and stamped received by the Sinaloa State Congress that day, does not say when Rocha plans to return or why he is stepping away again.
MEXICAN SENATOR ACCUSES SHEINBAUM OF SHIELDING 'NARCO-POLITICIANS' AFTER US CARTEL INDICTMENT

Sinaloa Gov. Ruben Rocha Moya speaks as he leaves the inauguration ceremony of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum in Mexico City, Mexico, on Oct. 1, 2024. (Jose Luis Torales/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
The request came just a day after Rocha announced his return and said it was his "duty to fulfill the mandate" of voters who elected him to serve through Oct. 31, 2027.
"Today, I return to the exercise of my responsibility as Governor of Sinaloa with a clear conscience and head held high, with the strength of truth on our side," Rocha wrote Friday on X.
Rocha said he spent 112 days away from office while making himself available to Mexican authorities investigating what he called "false accusations" by the U.S. government.
He said he personally appeared before Mexico’s Attorney General’s Office and answered investigators’ questions.

Rocha insisted the investigation had produced no evidence that he committed a crime and accused political opponents in Mexico and abroad of trying to damage both the country’s sovereignty and the left-wing movement he represents.
MEXICAN PRESIDENT IN THE DARK ABOUT DRUG OPERATION AFTER WHICH US, MEXICAN OFFICIALS WERE KILLED
"I am unrelated to and innocent of the fabrications woven against me," Rocha wrote.
Rocha’s return Friday did not get a warm reception from Mexico’s ruling Morena party or the government of President Claudia Sheinbaum.

Morena said it had no advance knowledge of Rocha’s decision and distanced itself from the move, according to Reuters. Mexico’s Interior Ministry said returning to office was Rocha’s decision alone and noted that the attorney general’s investigation remained open.
5 MEXICAN CARTEL BOSSES CHARGED IN WEAPONS, DRUG TRAFFICKING, TIMESHARE FRAUD SCHEMES, DOJ SAYS
Sheinbaum also posted a pointed message on X.
"No personal interest can ever stand above the interests of the people and the Nation," she wrote.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum responded to Rocha's return to office on Saturday. (Daniel Cardenas/Getty Images)
"Mexico deserves public servants who understand that positions are temporary, but responsibility to the Nation is eternal," Sheinbaum added.

U.S. prosecutors charged Rocha and nine other current and former officials in April with drug trafficking and related weapons offenses. The current and former high-ranking government and law enforcement officials are alleged to have partnered with the Sinaloa cartel to distribute massive quantities of narcotics to the United States.
U.S. prosecutors charged Rocha and nine other current and former officials in April with drug trafficking and related weapons offenses linked to the Sinaloa cartel. (Solidago/Getty Images)
Rocha is the first sitting Mexican governor to face charges from the U.S., according to Reuters.

The case has strained relations between the U.S. and Mexico. Sheinbaum has called the charges foreign interference, while Mexico says Washington has not provided enough evidence to justify Rocha’s arrest or extradition.

title: Hormuz crisis hides a deeper oil threat that could outlast the war
summary: Art Berman warns that 8 million barrels shut in near the Strait of Hormuz may never fully recover, even after a ceasefire reopens the waterway.
story: Art Berman says millions of barrels of production remain shut in and warns some wells could take months to restart — while others may never fully recover.

As global attention remains fixed on tankers moving through the Strait of Hormuz, a petroleum geologist is warning that the more consequential energy story may be unfolding thousands of feet underground — and could continue long after any political agreement ends the fighting.

Art Berman, a petroleum geologist and energy consultant with more than four decades of industry experience, told Fox News Digital that millions of barrels of Persian Gulf oil production remain shut in and warned that restoring those wells is far more complicated than simply reopening the strategic waterway.
"This is potentially a kind of a world-changing event, even if we resolve the political issues," Berman said.

"The bigger story and the more important one long term is that 8 million barrels of Persian Gulf production is currently shut in and world production is down about 10 million barrels a day," Berman explained.

In an aerial view, Marathon Petroleum Corp's Los Angeles Refinery, one of the largest oil refineries in North America, operates as gas prices rocket upward due to worldwide oil supply disruptions caused by the U.S. and Israeli attack on Iran, on March 10, 2026 in Carson, California. (David McNew/Getty Images)

"We can move tankers around and we can obsess about, you know, are there 4 million barrels getting through or are there 6 million or 9 million or whatever the right number is," he added. "But eventually, those tankers have to be filled with oil."

A White House official, speaking on background, pointed to the sharp decline in oil prices following the signing of the MOU and said the Strait of Hormuz is open, with the U.S. naval blockade in full effect.

Berman's estimate of Gulf shut-ins is broadly consistent with the latest assessment from the International Energy Agency. The IEA said in its Aug. 12, 2026, Oil Market Report, "Gulf oil production rose by a further 2.5 mb/d in July to 23.9 mb/d, still 8.3 mb/d below pre-war levels."
Global oil supply remained 6.3 million bpd below year-earlier levels, according to the agency.
The U.S. Energy Information Administration offers a somewhat different estimate.

EIA assessed production shut-ins at an average 5.5 million bpd in July, while warning that continuing constraints on Hormuz transit had forced the agency to increase its forecast for shut-in production in August. EIA expects production and trade patterns to generally return to pre-conflict conditions in early 2027, but says some Gulf producers may not regain their previous output during its forecast period.
Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on Aug. 3, 2026. (Reuters)

The distinction is important because much of the public discussion has centered on what the industry calls the midstream problem — whether tankers can safely transport oil through Hormuz — while Berman argues that the upstream problem of producing the oil itself could prove more enduring.
"The very last thing in the world I ever want to do is to shut in a well," Berman told Fox News Digital.

Restarting a well requires restoring communication between equipment at the surface and reservoirs thousands of feet underground, he explained, and extended shutdowns can create complications inside the reservoir and well.
"This is not like turning on a switch for a light bulb," Berman said. "It's a complicated, high-risk, relatively long-term process, and we don't know the outcome."

Berman estimated that roughly 80% of affected wells could return close to their previous production levels, although he said that could take weeks or months. He said many of the remainder could require additional engineering work and some could ultimately produce at lower rates.
"Some of that production will never come back," he predicted.
Other energy analysts agree that restarting Gulf production presents substantial technical challenges. But Wood Mackenzie is more optimistic than Berman about the ultimate recovery.

Its analysis projects that fields affected by the Hormuz closure could return to approximately 70% of their previous production within three months and 90% within six months, assuming a controlled restart. The final roughly 1 million bpd could take considerably longer.
Oil tankers and cargo ships line up in the Strait of Hormuz as seen from Khor Fakkan, United Arab Emirates, Wednesday, March 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Altaf Qadri)
Berman also warned against assuming that a ceasefire or political agreement would immediately restore pre-war energy flows.

Shipowners, insurers and crews would first have to become confident that tankers could safely navigate the waterway, while other logistical and security issues could continue even after governments reached an agreement.
"A simple political agreement doesn't mean the problem's over," Berman said.
Berman's argument goes considerably further than predicting a slow oil-market recovery.
He contends that the Persian Gulf conflict represents a fundamental shock to the global energy and economic system — one whose consequences will persist even after the immediate crisis ends.

Asked about his comparison with the COVID-19 pandemic, Berman told Fox News Digital that the scale of oil production affected by the current crisis makes it comparable to the largest economic disruptions of recent years.
"This is not just a news cycle," Berman said. "This is potentially a kind of a world-changing event, even if we resolve the political issues."
IRAN DEAL CLOCK HITS ZERO AS TRUMP DEMANDS ‘WHITE FLAG’ WITH NEW PRESSURE CAMPAIGN LOOMING
The ConocoPhillips Oil Refinery is seen in Wilmington, California on April 11, 2026. (Etienne Laurent / AFP via Getty Images)
The United States is the world's largest oil producer, but Berman argues that does not isolate American consumers from the disruption.
"The oil market and the refined products market is global," he told Fox News Digital.

Berman noted that U.S. refineries require different grades of crude to produce the country's mix of gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other petroleum products, meaning domestic production alone cannot eliminate America's exposure to international markets.
"The problem for the U.S. isn't that we don't have enough oil, we almost do," Berman said. "It's that the oil we have isn't the right kind" for everything American refineries produce.

EIA reported July 15 that Hormuz disruptions had already pushed international buyers toward alternative sources of petroleum products, contributing to higher U.S. refinery margins, production and exports.

Whether that recovery proceeds as EIA expects or encounters the technical obstacles Berman warns about could determine how long the economic consequences of the conflict linger after the shooting stops.
For Berman, the question is no longer simply when tankers return to Hormuz. It is whether the global energy system that emerges afterward will ever operate quite the way it did before.

The White House pushed back on concerns that the disruption represents a lasting threat to U.S. energy security, pointing to record American production and blaming Iran for instability in the critical shipping corridor.

"Thanks to President Trump, the United States is now the world’s number-one producer and exporter of oil and gas. Record oil and gas production strengthens our energy independence and national security," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital.

"The Iranian regime’s terrorist actions in the Strait of Hormuz have proven that our allies need to invest in reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources and advance new partnerships with the United States that enhance the world’s energy security," Rogers added.
Children swim as ships are seen anchored in the Strait of Hormuz on August 10, 2026 off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. ( )
Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House, U.S. Energy Information Administration and Defense Intelligence Agency for comment.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: White House teleprompter operator ordered to pay $172K for placing bets on speeches
summary: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission announced the penalties for Gabriel Perez, who made the bets through Kalshi.
story: A teleprompter operator for President Donald Trump who made online prediction trades based on information from upcoming speeches has been ordered to pay $172,000, a federal agency said Friday night.
Gabriel Perez used “material, nonpublic information” he obtained through his job to place “trades” on a prediction market, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission said in a news release.
Perez was ordered to pay the money he made in profits, $107,539.02, as well as a civil penalty of $65,000.
He’s also banned from trading on prediction markets for three years, the CFTC said.
Perez made the trades through Kalshi. The CFTC said Kalshi assisted in the matter.

“A Kalshi surveillance investigation caught a White House staffer engaging in prohibited trading activity. Today this individual was subjected to penalties by the CFTC and by our exchange,” Bobby DeNault, Kalshi’s lead lawyer, said in a post on X.
“It doesn’t matter who you are: violate our rules or federal law and you will face the consequences,” he added.
The White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Friday night. Perez could not be reached for comment.
Add to Google
Add to Google

The CFTC called it a case of insider trading, adding that Perez traded “presidential mention market contracts, which are event contracts reflecting words or phrases the President may use during his speeches.”
Perez was a technical assistant to the president who had served as a teleprompter operator for Trump since 2016.
The CFTC cited what it called Perez’s “exemplary cooperation” in the case when announcing the fine and penalties Friday.
Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt in July called the online trades a breach of ethics and “deeply unfortunate and frankly a disgrace.”
Perez was placed on leave in July and Leavitt said at the time that “this individual will no longer be here.”

title: Death toll climbs to more than 600, with 2,400 still missing as rescue efforts continue
summary: The death toll from catastrophic flash floods and mudslides in Nepal rose to at least 626 on Saturday, as more than 2,400 people remained missing in the country, including around 90 Americans.
story: The death toll from catastrophic flash floods and mudslides in Nepal rose to at least 626 on Saturday, as more than 2,400 people remained missing in the country, including around 90 Americans.

Rescuers have struggled to reach devastated communities along the Nepal-Tibet border, with the scale of the disaster coming into view four days after the torrent of water, ice and debris swept through Himalayan valleys, destroying homes, bridges and other infrastructure.
As families wait for news about their relatives, damaged roads, power outages and fears of further flooding have hampered rescue efforts.

China has separately reported seven deaths and 554 people missing in its Tibet region, including hundreds of foreigners. It is unclear how much overlap there is between the Chinese and Nepali missing-person counts.
House nearly engulfed by Nepal floodwaters

The disaster began Wednesday when a massive chunk of ice and rock dozens of times larger than the Empire State Building broke off a mountaintop and triggered the catastrophic flooding, geologists said.

Videos from the hardest-hit border regions showed people running as the debris flow swallowed buildings and vehicles, devastated towns and settlements, and severed roads, power and communications. The suspected collapse of a melting glacier shook the ground so violently that seismic monitors initially registered it as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake.
The State Department said it is not aware of any confirmed American deaths, but the large number of U.S. citizens still unaccounted for has added to the growing uncertainty surrounding the disaster.

Among the missing are Murphy, Texas residents Raghu Rajan and Archana Suresh. The pair were expected to cross the China-Nepal border Wednesday morning when the floods hit. Their phones last pinged that morning near a bridge that washed away.
“We know the severity of it, but still, you know, there’s a ray of hope for us to find our loved ones,” Rajan’s sister-in-law Divya Chandrashekar told NBC Dallas-Fort Worth.

Deepak and Madhu Ahuja, Plano, Texas business owners who have been married for 34 years, were in the area for a religious journey to Mount Kailash, a sacred site for both Hindus and Buddhists. Their family is now desperately trying to find them while holding out hope that they survived.
“My first reaction was, ‘That cannot be true,’” Deepak’s brother Sushil Ahuja said. “They went there for a good cause, right? This cannot happen to them.”
The State Department has urged U.S. citizens “currently in, or recently traveling through Rasuwa or another affected area” to get in touch via KathmanduACS@state.gov.
A spokesperson said relatives seeking information about family members in Nepal “should call 1-888-407-4747 toll-free from the United States and Canada, or 1-202-501-4444 from other locations.”
On Saturday, helicopters resumed operations in Nepal’s flood-hit Nuwakot district after poor weather temporarily halted efforts.

Some helicopters arrived loaded with boxes and bags of aid, including clothes, instant noodles, crackers and rice, while others returned from the flood-hit areas carrying survivors, among them several babies from the nearby community of Trishuli.
Meanwhile, China’s Ministry of Emergency Management urgently dispatched five tunnel experts to join rescue efforts at a hydropower station tunnel in Nepal, Chinese state media reported on Saturday.
Scores of bodies recovered along the banks of the Trishuli and Narayani rivers have been brought to the city of Pokhara on Phewa Lake in central Nepal for identification.

At the Western Regional Hospital in Pokhara, a crowd of families gathered Friday outside the facility’s morgue as they anxiously waited to see if their loved ones might be among the dead being brought to the medical facility.
Inside the hospital, a digital display could be seen being set up to show photographs of the faces of some of the victims, in hopes that their loved ones might be able to identify them.
The display was set up by police, with authorities saying some of the bodies recovered from the floods were in an advanced state of decomposition, making physical identification difficult.
Meanwhile, rescuers are working “day and night” to search for survivors amid challenging conditions, a U.N. official said.

“The government has established a relief fund, and already the World Bank, India, China and the U.S. have committed to pledge $229 million to support,” Lila Pieters Yahia, the U.N. resident coordinator in Nepal, said, adding that the U.N. is also providing $2 million from its humanitarian relief fund for immediate assistance.
Nepal may need $4 billion to $5 billion to rebuild following the disaster, the country’s finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters on Saturday.

title: Tennessee moves to rename Nashville International Airport in Dolly Parton’s honor
summary: Nashville International Airport could soon be renamed after Tennessee icon Dolly Parton, the governor and airport announced Friday.
story: Nashville International Airport could soon be renamed after Tennessee icon Dolly Parton, the governor and airport announced Friday.
The beloved country legend and philanthropist, who hailed from rural Tennessee, died Tuesday at the age of 80.

The airport and Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee announced the intent to name the airport in her honor to create “a lasting tribute to her indelible legacy and the generations of people she inspired across Tennessee and around the world,” they said in a news release.
Lee spoke with Parton’s team about the proposal this week and they expressed “their appreciation,” the governor said.

“Dolly Parton’s extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state,” Lee said. “From her rural mountain home in East Tennessee to global stages, Dolly carried the Volunteer Spirit with her. At a place where Tennessee welcomes the world, it is fitting that Nashville International Airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith, and kindness.”
The proposal to rename the airport will be addressed at the Metro Nashville Airport Authority’s meeting Sept. 17.

A petition to rename the airport in honor of Parton, which was started more than a year before her death, has over 160,000 signatures as of Friday night and also garnered responses in support from a Nashville City Council member and a Tennesseee state representative.

The “Queen of Country” died surrounded by loved ones following a brief battle with cancer. Her death was felt across the nation and the world, and inspired heartfelt tributes from fans, celebrities and politicians alike.

Known beyond her music for her extravagant blonde hairdos, Southern charm, wit, generosity and kindness, Parton was beloved by generations. She was also a keen businesswoman and devoted philanthropist, creating the Dollywood Foundation for property relief and educational programs in East Tennessee, as well as Imagination Library, which mails free books to children around the world.

title: White House teleprompter operator ordered to pay $172K for placing bets on speeches
summary: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission announced the penalties for Gabriel Perez, who made the bets through Kalshi.
story: A teleprompter operator for President Donald Trump who made online prediction trades based on information from upcoming speeches has been ordered to pay $172,000, a federal agency said Friday night.
Gabriel Perez used “material, nonpublic information” he obtained through his job to place “trades” on a prediction market, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission said in a news release.
Perez was ordered to pay the money he made in profits, $107,539.02, as well as a civil penalty of $65,000.
He’s also banned from trading on prediction markets for three years, the CFTC said.
Perez made the trades through Kalshi. The CFTC said Kalshi assisted in the matter.

“A Kalshi surveillance investigation caught a White House staffer engaging in prohibited trading activity. Today this individual was subjected to penalties by the CFTC and by our exchange,” Bobby DeNault, Kalshi’s lead lawyer, said in a post on X.
“It doesn’t matter who you are: violate our rules or federal law and you will face the consequences,” he added.
The White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Friday night. Perez could not be reached for comment.
Add to Google
Add to Google

The CFTC called it a case of insider trading, adding that Perez traded “presidential mention market contracts, which are event contracts reflecting words or phrases the President may use during his speeches.”
Perez was a technical assistant to the president who had served as a teleprompter operator for Trump since 2016.
The CFTC cited what it called Perez’s “exemplary cooperation” in the case when announcing the fine and penalties Friday.
Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt in July called the online trades a breach of ethics and “deeply unfortunate and frankly a disgrace.”
Perez was placed on leave in July and Leavitt said at the time that “this individual will no longer be here.”

title: Trump says he’ll visit Pentagon rather than Ground Zero for 9/11 ceremony
summary: President Donald Trump will appear at the Pentagon to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks on Sept.
story: President Donald Trump will appear at the Pentagon to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, instead of visiting Ground Zero in New York City.
Asked about why he would not be commemorating the anniversary in his hometown, Trump told reporters Friday, “Because I’m going to the Pentagon.”

Vice President JD Vance is instead expected to attend the event in New York City, according to a senior administration official. Other officials will attend a ceremony in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, on the day, the official added.

The New York Times first reported that Trump would travel to the Pentagon on 9/11, writing Thursday that the president had initially wanted to go to New York City but decided against it when organizers would not allow him to speak during the Ground Zero program, which traditionally does not permit speeches.
The White House has denied that claim, with White House communications director Steven Cheung calling the report “FAKE NEWS” in a post on X Friday.
A senior administration official also told reporters Friday that the report was “false” but would not explain further.

“As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement. “On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans.”
Trump visited the Pentagon on 9/11 last year before traveling to New York City to spend the evening at a New York Yankees game that honored the victims of the attacks.

He did attend the ceremony at Ground Zero in 2024, appearing at the event where his presidential opponent, then-Vice President Kamala Harris, and President Joe Biden were also in attendance. Trump had last gone to the New York City ceremony in 2016, but did visit a fire station and police precinct in the city in 2021.
During his first term, Trump spent the anniversaries at the Pentagon in 2017 and 2019 and went to Shanksville, Pennsylvania, in 2018 and 2020.

title: How Lindsay Clancy sought help before she killed her three children
summary: In the months before Lindsay Clancy killed her three children and tried to take her own life, she was desperate for help — she saw psychiatrists, called a suicide hotline, went to the emergency room and was turned away from inpatient treatment.
story: In the months before Lindsay Clancy killed her three children and tried to take her own life, she was desperate for help — she saw psychiatrists, called a suicide hotline, went to the emergency room and was turned away from inpatient treatment. She was put on 13 medications over four months as providers sought to treat her ongoing symptoms and adverse reactions to the medications.
Clancy, 36, is accused of murdering her three children — Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months — on Jan. 24, 2023, before she threw herself out her bedroom window in a suicide attempt.

Prosecutors spent nearly six weeks presenting their case to jurors in the murder trial. They called 70 witnesses in an attempt to show that the mother planned the deaths, driving her husband from home so she could carry out the acts.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Her defense attorneys have said that Clancy was in the grips of postpartum psychosis, a rare condition that can alter new mothers’ sense of reality and is considered a psychiatric emergency. Her condition, they told jurors, compelled her to act on the voices in her head that were telling her to kill her three children and herself. For months, she had been seeking help from doctors and medical professionals.
The prosecution and defense made their closing arguments Thursday, and the jury began deliberating that afternoon.

The trial has raised questions about the type of care Clancy received. Clancy’s medical providers have said they adjusted her treatment as needed and based on her responses to the medications she was prescribed. At times, the medical providers testified, they did not have full access to her medical record and did not coordinate with one another. It was also unclear when Clancy stopped taking medications and began to take new ones.

Dr. Veerle Bergink, the director of Mount Sinai’s Women’s Mental Health Center, told NBC News that testimony about Clancy’s providers shows that “during multiple occasions, the diagnosis was missed and she did not get the right treatment.” Bergink, who specializes in mental health during pregnancy and postpartum, said Clancy’s adverse reaction to the antidepressants she was taking could have been “a major clue” that her diagnosis went beyond postpartum depression and that she needed different medication for postpartum psychosis.

Dr. Tracy Moran Vozar, a psychologist and perinatal mental health expert, said Clancy’s case exemplifies the systemic issues and lack of communication across the healthcare system, especially when it comes to patients with serious mental illness who see multiple providers across different systems. Neither doctor personally treated Clancy.
“It’s very tragic, of course, for her, her family, and everything that happened,” Bergink said. “But it’s a tragedy for doctors, as well.”
Court testimony and documents from the trial provide a timeline of the care Clancy sought and received in the months before the killings.
September 2022

On Sept. 15, 2022, Clancy first met with Dr. Jennifer Tufts, a psychiatrist at Aster Mental Health, more than three months after her youngest child, Callan, was born. Tufts treated Clancy through January 2023. Clancy reported she was experiencing anxiety attacks, depressed mood, being unable to feel pleasure, guilt, decreased appetite, racing thoughts and other symptoms, Tufts testified in court. She said Clancy responded “no” to questions about whether she was hearing voices or having thoughts about harming herself or others.

Tufts diagnosed Clancy with generalized anxiety disorder and an adjustment disorder with depressed mood, which is when someone is reacting or struggling with a stressful change more intensely than expected.

She also prescribed Clancy a standard dose of the antidepressant sertraline, known by the brand name Zoloft, at a dose of 25 milligrams, then increased to 50 mg. Tufts testified that Clancy had previously taken Zoloft for about a week after the birth of her second child, according to NBC Boston.
October

Tufts testified that in October, Clancy felt “awful” after her dose of Zoloft was increased and that she was feeling more depressed, “crying all day” and having trouble eating and sleeping, among other symptoms, according to NBC Boston.

“Anxiety was really bad even before med, now hard to differentiate. Overnight racing thoughts, paranoid of getting suicidal thoughts, something bad happening. Doesn’t want to be alone,” Tufts said, reading from her records, according to NBC Boston. Tufts said she was “very concerned” about Clancy at this point. She told Clancy to stop taking the Zoloft.

Through the end of the month, Tufts and Clancy met again, and she was prescribed the benzodiazepine lorazepam, known by the brand name Ativan, the anti-anxiety medication buspirone and the antihistamine hydroxyzine, according to the defense and court testimony.
Add to Google
Add to Google
November

Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington said at the trial that Clancy had gotten much worse by the next appointment on Nov. 2, despite the medications she was taking, according to NBC Boston. Reddington said Tufts said that Clancy’s insomnia had increased, that she had anxiety and that she was worrying about suicide.

Tufts testified that during that appointment, she said Clancy was “improving” and therefore decreased the Ativan, according to NBC Boston. Tufts responded to Reddington that she did not recall that the symptoms were significantly aggravated. On Nov. 16, Clancy went to the South Shore Hospital emergency room, where she was prescribed the antidepressant trazodone.

Days later, on Nov. 21, psychiatric nurse practitioner Julie Paul saw Clancy at South Shore Perinatal Behavioral Health clinic after Clancy’s former mother-in-law contacted the doctor, according to NBC Boston. Paul prescribed the antidepressant fluoxetine, known under the brand name Prozac, at 10 mg.
Lindsay Clancy denied care by crisis hotline, psychiatrist says

Paul testified that during this time, Clancy “was feeling overwhelmed” and that she had increased anxiety as her husband returned to work after the birth of their child. Clancy also described having issues with sleeping. During a follow-up visit the next day, Tufts testified, Clancy denied having any suicidal ideation.

On Nov. 25, Paul prescribed Clancy the antidepressant mirtazapine, known by the brand name Remeron, at 5 mg; the benzodiazepine clonazepam, known as the brand name Klonopin, at 0.5 mg; and the anti-insomnia medication zolpidem, known by the brand name Ambien, according to the defense. At this time, Clancy also reported having had an adverse reaction to Prozac, according to the defense. Clancy told Paul she was feeling disconnected and “spacey” after having taken the medication, according to Paul’s testimony, so they switched to mirtazapine.

Clancy reported dissociation and confusion to her care team on Nov. 28 after having taken Remeron, according to a defense timeline of when Clancy sought care. Two days later, psychiatric nurse practitioner Rebecca Jollotta prescribed the antipsychotic Seroquel at 25 mg. Jollotta took over Clancy’s care after Paul left South Shore Perinatal Behavioral Health clinic.
December

In December, Clancy also continued meeting with Tufts. As her symptoms continued, she called a suicide crisis hotline and sought inpatient treatment — which she was turned away from, according to the defense and trial testimony.
Tufts said that during a visit on Dec. 1, Clancy denied feeling suicidal but felt “close to being suicidal.”
Clancy said she was having difficulty sleeping because of the multiple medications she was taking, Tufts said.
Clancy told Tufts she had “worse depression and intrusive thoughts” after having taken Remeron, along with “the feeling that I was going to die,” according to court testimony.
Reddington, Clancy’s lawyer, asked Tufts at the trial, “You’ve got a woman telling you she’s hopeless, she doesn’t care if she dies, she can’t sleep. What did you do to validate your therapy?”
“I told her that this was something we could address, there was hope, there were treatments,” Tufts replied, according to NBC Boston.
They also discussed the possibility of undiagnosed bipolar disorder, with Tufts testifying that Clancy did not appear to have mania at the time.

On Dec. 2, Clancy returned to the South Shore Hospital behavioral clinic. Latiesha Dukes, a perinatal clinician who provided short-term therapy for Clancy, said that during her intake appointment, Clancy presented with concerns of anxiety, lack of sleep and thoughts of wanting to die, according to NBC Boston.
Dukes testified that Clancy reported “having low mood and feeling numb” during the appointment.

She said she met with Clancy four times and did not observe any signs of mania or psychosis. She said she referred Clancy to Women & Infants Hospital in Rhode Island because of “continued passive suicidal ideation.” Clancy went to the hospital but was discharged.

On Dec. 4, Clancy called a suicide crisis hotline. She met with Dukes again the next day and told her that she had called the Aspire crisis line and was evaluated by a clinician but was told “she did not meet the criteria for inpatient treatment due to not having any suicidal ideation plan,” Dukes testified.
From Dec. 6 to Dec. 13, Jollotta prescribed the benzodiazepine diazepam, known by the brand name Valium, at different doses and also increased Clancy’s Seroquel dose.
Days later, on Dec. 15, Patrick Clancy contacted providers to report worsening symptoms, according to the defense’s timeline chart.
The next day, Clancy met with Tufts, when, according to Tufts’ testimony, Clancy was “sleeping but she was still feeling very poorly.”
What is postpartum psychosis? Inside the Lindsay Clancy case

Tufts testified that Clancy continued to feel hopeless and depressed and had some suicidal ideation but that she denied having a plan to hurt herself. Tufts prescribed the mood stabilizer lamotrigine, known by the brand name Lamictal.
“While she was certainly struggling, she did not require hospitalization at that point,” Tufts said, according to NBC Boston.
Reddington asked Tufts on the stand whether she knew Clancy had told her then-husband that she was having thoughts about harming the children, according to NBC Boston.
“I would have been very concerned if I had heard that,” Tufts said.
On Dec. 19, Jollotta increased Clancy’s Seroquel dose. The next day, Clancy visited the Massachusetts General Hospital emergency room, according to a chart from the defense.

Over the next few days, she was evaluated for and participated in the Women and Infants Partial Hospitalization Program for patients with postpartum depression, according to the defense’s chart. Jollotta lowered Clancy’s Seroquel dose.
But by Dec. 30, Clancy had returned to the Massachusetts General Hospital emergency room, according to the defense’s chart.
January 2023

On New Year’s Day, Clancy arrived at McLean Hospital from the emergency department at Massachusetts General Hospital. Dr. Alia Goodheart, a psychiatrist, testified that Clancy’s main complaint was that she was having trouble sleeping and felt “numb,” according to NBC Boston. Clancy also complained that she was having side effects from the medication she was taking.
Two days later, Clancy met Goodheart for the first time. Goodheart testified that Clancy said she was feeling “numbness” but did not indicate any plan for suicide, according to NBC Boston.
Goodheart said in court that the potential for a bipolar disorder diagnosis came up during the sessions.
She said she did not observe signs of psychosis from Clancy.
On Jan. 5, Clancy left McLean Hospital. She had been prescribed trazodone and Ativan. Goodheart testified that she did not have concerns about her safety or worry that she was a risk to anyone else.

Clancy had an appointment with Tufts the day after she left McLean Hospital. She was diagnosed with “major depression,” Tufts said at the trial, according to NBC Boston. She continued to report numbness and having trouble sleeping, Tufts testified.

From Jan. 9 through Jan. 16, Tufts adjusted Clancy’s prescriptions, including prescribing her Valium at different doses and trazadone, and Jollotta also prescribed her Valium, according to the defense’s chart.

On Jan. 16, Clancy had another appointment with Tufts, who prescribed the antidepressant amitriptyline. Clancy again told Tufts she was feeling numb and that bonding with her infant son felt forced, Tufts testified, according to NBC Boston. Tufts said she was “concerned that she was depressed.”

Clancy had her last appointment with Tufts on Jan. 23. Tufts testified that Clancy still had a depressed mood and felt numb and that she said she had to force herself out of bed, according to NBC Boston. Tufts testified that Clancy reported no signs of suicidal or homicidal ideation and showed no signs of psychosis.
The next day, authorities allege, she killed her three children and tried to die by suicide.

If you or someone you know is struggling or in emotional distress, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For additional resources, visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

title: Trump says U.S. has struck deal with Venezuela to take control of 65 billion barrels of oil reserves
summary: President Donald Trump announced Friday that the U.S. had entered into an agreement with Venezuela to take control of the country’s 65 billion barrels of oil reserves.
story: President Donald Trump announced Friday that the U.S. had entered into an agreement with Venezuela to take control of the country’s 65 billion barrels of oil reserves.

“BREAKING NEWS: The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY! At my direction, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, working closely with Highly Respected Interim President of Venezuela, Delcy Rodriguez, and, through a partnership with private business, have secured majority U.S. control of more than 65 BILLION BARRELS of proven Oil Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American Taxpayer,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Trump added that the transaction “MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves.”
In January, the U.S. military carried out an operation to capture Venezuela’s President Nicolás Maduro to face federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges in the U.S.
Trump is facing increasing pressure as the midterms loom and gas prices have spiked because of the war with Iran, which the U.S. and Israel started exactly six months ago.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio touted the deal as a “huge win” for both the U.S. and Venezuela in a post on X.

“It demonstrates how President Trump’s bold foreign policy is driving America First wins: securing stable reserves and low-cost oil in our Hemisphere and lowering gas prices here at home,” he wrote. “For the Venezuelan people, this deal will bring nearly $100 billion in private investment, support thousands of high-paying jobs, and drive the reconstruction of Venezuela’s economy.”

Venezuela has among the largest oil reserves in the world, with an estimated 303 billion barrels of crude oil in the ground. That’s about 17% of the world’s supply, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Unlike other parts of the world, where geologists have to search for untapped oil, the reserves under Venezuela’s soil are largely mapped and known, experts say. But because of dilapidated infrastructure, the country only produces about 1% of the world’s oil.

title: Elon Musk enters the midterm chat: From the Politics Desk
summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
In today’s edition, we dive into Elon Musk’s first foray into this year’s midterms. Plus, Kristen Welker digs into how voters are feeling about the Iran war six months in.
Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.
Elon Musk enters the midterm chat
Elon Musk is back.
The tech billionaire’s super PAC launched digital ads this month in three states with key Senate races: Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire.
The effort from America PAC targets specific lists of people and urges viewers to register to vote, according to a review of Meta political ad data.

Some ads are generic, featuring reminders that the Senate races in their states could decide control of the chamber. Others go on the attack against socialism, including one ad that features an image of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, warning that “if you don’t vote in November, socialism could declare victory over America.”

The campaign marks America PAC’s first significant ad spending since the April 2025 Wisconsin Supreme Court election. Musk injected himself into the center of that race, spending millions of dollars and traveling to the state. But his endorsed candidate, conservative Brad Schimel, ultimately fell well short of Susan Crawford, allowing liberals to maintain their majority on the swing state court.

Musk spent a quarter-billion dollars to boost Trump and the GOP in the 2024 election. He then went on to serve as an adviser to Trump at the outset of his second term, before having an on-again, off-again relationship with the president after leaving the White House.

It remains to be seen exactly how much Musk will spend this time around. But as the Republicans prepare to face a daunting political environment this fall, any financial involvement from Musk in battleground contests will be a welcome development for the party.
Read more →
Voter frustrations with Trump and the GOP reshape the midterm map

As the war with Iran hits the six-month mark, Americans appear to have reached a consensus: They don’t support it. That was the case when the war started, and it remains so in recent polling over the last few weeks.

Poll after poll shows that President Donald Trump’s handling of the war is deeply underwater and that voters are skeptical it will come to an end any time soon. It’s a reminder of the political headwinds Trump and Republicans face across multiple fronts. In addition to this conflict, Trump continues to escalate trade wars with countries like Canada, while capturing headlines for trying to rename Lake Ontario or threatening to demolish the Kennedy Center.

We’ve spoken with voters across the country who keep making the same point — they’re laser-focused on the economy and frustrated about the war, with many worried the administration’s efforts aren’t hitting the mark.

Those frustrations are one reason why even traditionally red states like Texas — the home of one of my guests this Sunday, Republican Sen. Ted Cruz — appears to be in play this cycle. Democratic state Rep. James Talarico is waging a tough battle there against state Attorney General Ken Paxton in what’s become a major proving ground for so many of these issues.

Most recently, Talarico has blasted Trump’s effort to suspend tariffs on beef exports as part of a broader attempt to hit the GOP on the issue of rising costs. But that issue in particular has scrambled the usual party lines: A chorus of Republican lawmakers around the country has also warned the plan could hurt American farmers and ranchers.

Paxton, meanwhile, has countered with an affordability pitch of his own centered on lowering taxes, as he and Trump try to frame Talarico as too extreme on social issues. In a sign of how competitive the race has become, Trump also traveled to the state for a fundraiser yesterday.
Cruz and Rep. James Clyburn, D-S.C., will join me on “Meet the Press” this Sunday to discuss all of this and more.

There are comparable Labor Day sales online and in stores, especially at big box retailers, so you’re guaranteed to find strong deals wherever you shop. A few things to keep in mind while deciding whether to leave your couch:

Shopping online makes comparing prices and stacking savings easier, letting you consider the total value of a deal, not just the sale price, says Ashley Feinstein Gerstley, a shopping and savings expert at Rakuten. Open a few tabs and search for the exact same product at a handful of retailers to weigh which one offers the lowest price and lowest shipping fee. You can also shop through cash back apps and browser extensions online, which help you find additional promo codes and rewards, she says.Shopping in stores lets you try out big ticket items like furniture, mattresses and major appliances, giving you more confidence in pricey purchases. You can also ask a store associate about lower-priced floor models and open-box inventory, which you may never see advertised online, says Carls.Shipping fees add up, especially if you’re placing online orders at numerous retailers or buying big-ticket products that require installation. Some early Labor Day sales have already started, but the majority of them begin between Tuesday, Sept. 1 and Friday, Sept. 4. Retailers typically consider the Friday before the official holiday, which lands on Monday, Sept. 7 this year, the start of the long weekend, so all sales will be live by Sept. 4.

Plan for most Labor Day sales to end on the holiday, Monday, Sept. 7. Some may extend longer into the week, but don’t plan on it — aim to get all your shopping done by Labor Day, but shop sooner if you can, says Carls. “Summer clearance is already working with fewer sizes, colors and models, so the thing you actually want can disappear before the promotion does,” she says. “The discount may hang around, but your exact patio set, for example, may not.”

All the experts I talked to agree that the best way to save the most money during Labor Day sales is to stack your savings. That means looking at the deal price as the starting point and combining it with additional offers to save even more, says Gerstley. For example, search for promo codes to lower prices further, shop through cash back apps and browsers to put money back in your pocket, and pay with credit cards that let you earn rewards as you spend.

Additionally, make sure you’re comparing prices across retailers before buying anything, says Porwal. Since so many retailers are hosting sales right now, they’re all competing for your attention, and you never know when one might lower prices just a little bit more to give themselves an edge, or throw in extras that make a purchase more worthwhile, like free shipping, delivery, install or haul-away. Don’t be afraid to ask about price matching, too, says Carls. If a retailer really wants your business, they’ll be open to negotiating with you.

Last but not least, don’t feel like you absolutely have to buy something if deals aren’t compelling, says Gerstley. As we enter the final quarter of the year, sales are plentiful with early Black Friday and Cyber Monday offers starting in October, and Amazon Prime Big Deal Days might be around the corner (it hasn’t been confirmed yet, however). There will be more promotional moments in the near future, and waiting might be key to maximizing your savings.
