title: ICE arrests far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos
summary: The far-right commentator and self-described internet troll was arrested at the airport in New Orleans for staying in the country after his visa expired, according to DHS.
story: Milo Yiannopoulos, a self-described libertarian and professional internet troll who became known for his controversial right-wing political views, is in ICE custody.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News that ICE arrested Yiannopoulos, a United Kingdom national, on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Kenner, Louisiana.
The DHS spokesperson said Yiannopoulos legally entered the U.S. on May 14, 2019, through New York City, but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws.”

Yiannopoulos was taken into ICE custody Thursday after “failing to show up for his immigration hearing” on July 22, prompting an immigration judge to issue a final order of removal against him, according to the spokesperson. “He will remain in ICE custody pending removal,” the spokesperson added.
TMZ first reported Yiannopoulos’ ICE arrest.

Yiannopoulos has ties to Kanye West, known now as Ye, and  previously served as the rapper’s chief of staff when Ye tried to run for president in 2020 and 2024. He also worked at Ye’s clothing brand Yeezy, but resigned from that job two years ago after the singer announced he was launching an adult entertainment studio under his Yeezy brand, TMZ reported.
Ye is scheduled to perform in Louisiana Friday night at the New Orleans Caesars Superdome. It’s unclear whether Yiannopoulos was in the state to attend the concert.

A former editor for Breitbart, the conservative internet publication President Donald Trump once considered one of his favorite news sources, Yiannopoulos resigned from the role in 2017 amid backlash to his reported comments about teens and sexual abuse.
The DHS spokesperson said that the Trump administration is “working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”

title: Tennessee moves to rename Nashville International Airport in Dolly Parton’s honor
summary: Nashville International Airport could soon be renamed after Tennessee icon Dolly Parton, the governor and airport announced Friday.
story: Nashville International Airport could soon be renamed after Tennessee icon Dolly Parton, the governor and airport announced Friday.
The beloved country legend and philanthropist, who hailed from rural Tennessee, died Tuesday at the age of 80.

The airport and Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee announced the intent to name the airport in her honor to create “a lasting tribute to her indelible legacy and the generations of people she inspired across Tennessee and around the world,” they said in a news release.
Lee spoke with Parton’s team about the proposal this week and they expressed “their appreciation,” the governor said.

“Dolly Parton’s extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state,” Lee said. “From her rural mountain home in East Tennessee to global stages, Dolly carried the Volunteer Spirit with her. At a place where Tennessee welcomes the world, it is fitting that Nashville International Airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith, and kindness.”
The proposal to rename the airport will be addressed at the Metro Nashville Airport Authority’s meeting Sept. 17.

A petition to rename the airport in honor of Parton, which was started more than a year before her death, has over 160,000 signatures as of Friday night and also garnered responses in support from a Nashville City Council member and a Tennesseee state representative.

The “Queen of Country” died surrounded by loved ones following a brief battle with cancer. Her death was felt across the nation and the world, and inspired heartfelt tributes from fans, celebrities and politicians alike.

Known beyond her music for her extravagant blonde hairdos, Southern charm, wit, generosity and kindness, Parton was beloved by generations. She was also a keen businesswoman and devoted philanthropist, creating the Dollywood Foundation for property relief and educational programs in East Tennessee, as well as Imagination Library, which mails free books to children around the world.

title: Trump says he’ll visit Pentagon rather than Ground Zero for 9/11 ceremony
summary: President Donald Trump will appear at the Pentagon to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks on Sept.
story: President Donald Trump will appear at the Pentagon to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, instead of visiting Ground Zero in New York City.
Asked about why he would not be commemorating the anniversary in his hometown, Trump told reporters Friday, “Because I’m going to the Pentagon.”

Vice President JD Vance is instead expected to attend the event in New York City, according to a senior administration official. Other officials will attend a ceremony in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, on the day, the official added.

The New York Times first reported that Trump would travel to the Pentagon on 9/11, writing Thursday that the president had initially wanted to go to New York City but decided against it when organizers would not allow him to speak during the Ground Zero program, which traditionally does not permit speeches.
The White House has denied that claim, with White House communications director Steven Cheung calling the report “FAKE NEWS” in a post on X Friday.
A senior administration official also told reporters Friday that the report was “false” but would not explain further.

“As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement. “On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans.”
Trump visited the Pentagon on 9/11 last year before traveling to New York City to spend the evening at a New York Yankees game that honored the victims of the attacks.

He did attend the ceremony at Ground Zero in 2024, appearing at the event where his presidential opponent, then-Vice President Kamala Harris, and President Joe Biden were also in attendance. Trump had last gone to the New York City ceremony in 2016, but did visit a fire station and police precinct in the city in 2021.
During his first term, Trump spent the anniversaries at the Pentagon in 2017 and 2019 and went to Shanksville, Pennsylvania, in 2018 and 2020.

title: Judge blocks Trump’s Postal Service regulation on mail-in ballots
summary: The judge said the regulation is most likely unlawful because the president can’t insert the federal government into elections without Congress’ approval.
story: A federal judge Thursday blocked a Postal Service regulation that would exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections in the latest setback on the issue for President Donald Trump.

The recently finalized measure would implement a key provision of Trump’s executive order on mail-in ballots that would add a new level of bureaucracy to the elections process, which is typically administered by states.
The executive order directed the U.S. Postal Service to, among other things, track mail-in ballots and potentially reject those submitted by people not on a federal list of eligible voters.

The decision by Boston-based U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in one case brought by the League of Women Voters and other groups and another brought by a coalition of states means part of the executive order remains blocked for at least 14 days, with time running out to implement it ahead of the November election.

“This rule is a clear attempt by the federal government to interfere in elections it has no power to control,” New York Attorney General Letitia James said in a statement. “Today, a federal court halted it before this administration could wreak havoc on our elections.”
Talwani wrote that the regulation is most likely unlawful because the president cannot insert the federal government into elections without the express authorization of Congress.
“The court finds plaintiffs likely to succeed on the merits of their claims,” she said.
The Trump administration could seek to quickly overturn her decision by rushing to the Supreme Court.
Trump often criticizes mail-in ballots, claiming without evidence that there is rampant fraud even though they are widely used by Republicans and Democrats all across the country.
Talwani noted in her ruling that the administration had not offered “any evidence regarding fraudulent absentee or mail-in voting.”
The government’s interest in “correcting an unsubstantiated problem through likely unconstitutional means is dwarfed by the overwhelming risk of pervasive disenfranchisement,” she added.

Directly addressing the short time frame ahead of the election, Talwani said states “have neither time nor funds” to meet the necessary requirements, including updating election management systems and training staff members.
Based on the evidence before her, states’ compliance with what the Trump administration is asking of them before the 2026 midterms would be “practically impossible,” Talwani wrote.
In a separate decision Wednesday, Talwani lifted an earlier injunction she had imposed that blocked vital elements of Trump’s executive order in the case.
It is a different injunction from the one the Supreme Court lifted Monday in a similar case brought by California and 22 other states. Talwani is overseeing both cases.
The Supreme Court found that Talwani had acted too hastily in ruling on the executive order but did not weigh in on whether the underlying proposal or the Postal Service regulation is lawful.

While the Postal Service regulation is now blocked, a provision of the executive order requiring the Department of Homeland Security to compile lists of eligible voters and send them to states remains in effect.

title: He Lived 10 Minutes From Where Dolly Parton Grew Up. She Helped Him Attend His Dream School
summary: Growing up in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, Dolly Parton was always a part of Gavin Harper’s life.
story: Growing up in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, Dolly Parton was always a part of Gavin Harper’s life.

The small mountain town is only 10 miles from Dollywood and about 16 from Locust Ridge, where Parton grew up. Earlier this year, Harper found out he had been chosen as the recipient of the 2026 Dolly Parton Scholarship, making his connection to the iconic late superstar even sweeter.

“Somebody should have told this kid in 12 years he’d be chasing dreams he doesn’t even know he has yet,” he wrote on Instagram in May, alongside a video sharing the news. “Thank you @dollyparton for helping make this kid’s dream come true.”
Parton died at the age 80 on Aug. 25, with fans and friends mourning the country icon, including Harper who posted a musical tribute to his “inspiration.”
In his video, he performs her 1987 song “Wildflowers” and notes that without Parton he “literally wouldn’t be where I am today.”

He recently started as a freshman at Belmont University in Nashville, telling NBC News that the $15,000 he got from the Dolly Parton Scholarship was the last bit he needed to attend his dream school where he’s studying songwriting.

“Dolly’s been a huge thing for me. And when I got in my freshman year (of high school), I fell in love with music completely,” Harper says, sharing he then knew he wanted to be a musician. “... And the best person I could look to was Dolly Parton because she grew up 10 minutes from my house.”

He shares how Parton was “everything” to his community. He says his brother was born at the Dolly Parton Birthing Unit at Covenant Health LeConte in Sevierville, Tennessee, and he attended elementary school “where all of her nieces and nephews went.” He was also part of Parton’s Imagination Library, which sends out free children’s books every month.
“I used to call her the Book Lady because she would always send books,” he says. “That’s just how I knew her as when I was young.”
When he was 14, he played at The Pines Downtown in Sevierville, “where Dolly played her first paid show when she was 10,” he says.
“I remember my mom made a huge deal of that, and it meant nothing to me at the time because I just didn’t understand it,” Harper recalls. “But now that means the world to me.”

This past year, he decided to apply to The Dolly Parton Scholarship, which is part of The Dollywood Foundation. The scholarship provides funds to students who “have a dream they wish to pursue and who can successfully communicate their plan and commitment to realize their dreams,” per the website.
Now enrolled in his first year of college and in the songwriting program, Harper is grateful for the opportunities Parton and the scholarship provided him.
“I just hope one day I can be as big an artist as Dolly,” he says. “And I hope that I can also give back to my community and be a good influence on the world.”

title: Justus Kelley Reacts to Being the 1st Miss USA to Be a Married Mom in Her 30s
summary: Justus Kelley made history as Miss USA winner who is a mom, wife and woman in her 30s. Here’s what to know.
story: Justus Kelley just made history as Miss USA 2026. She’s the first married woman, and the first woman in her 30s to win the pageant, Miss USA confirmed to TODAY.com.
The day after the Miss Virginia winner was crowned Miss USA 2026 on Aug. 27, Kelley tells TODAY.com what the moment of being crowned felt like.

“I feel like I left my heart on that stage, and I was so proud of what I had done this week, not just on stage, but each piece of how I decided to show up, bringing a message with me, doing everything with purpose and a mission in mind,” Kelley says.
“That, for me, is what I came to do, and so I really did feel like no matter what happens, I feel like I won. I just felt so much peace. I felt contentment.”
Until recent rule changes in 2023 and 2024, Miss USA prohibited women who were over the age of 28, or who were mothers, pregnant, married or divorced from entering the pageant.
As part of Miss USA’s 75th year celebration, Kelley was joined on stage by legacy queens.
“What we’re doing is only because of the shoulders that we’re standing on, the people that came before us,” Kelley says of meeting the legacy queens.

“I literally had to do my best to contain my excitement all week as I was meeting different former Miss USA’s, just in disbelief that I was meeting them in real life,” Kelley says. “These are women that I follow on social media and have followed throughout the years, and have looked up to them for so much of my life. So to now have these women be people that are welcoming me into a sisterhood just felt like a dream.”

Kelley is a foster parent. She and her husband, Tyler Kelley, are currently foster parents to a sibling set and have fostered previous children. Kelley is also the founder of Foster Footprints, a DMV-based foster support program.
She says she looks at her pageants, and the newest title, as a bigger way to raise awareness about the realities of foster care.
“I went to Miss USA, and I thought, how can I be intentional about my message and my purpose? Just being embedded in everything that I do,” she says.

“I’m very honest and transparent with people about how much I’ve learned since becoming a foster parent,” Kelley adds. “I had a little bit of an ignorance as to what kids would experience. I kind of assumed that every child in this situation must come from an awful situation or an awful parent. And my reality and what I’ve seen from the kiddos that have come into my home is they are coming oftentimes from families that deeply love them but are struggling, have fallen on hard times, are having housing crises and dealing with addiction.”

Kelley’s commitment to shedding light on the realities of the U.S. foster care system is evident in her Miss USA campaign. As she traveled to Miami, where this year’s competition was hosted, she carried trash bags. In an Instagram post, she explained why.

“The trash bags I carry reflect a reality far too many foster children know all too well. A trash bag should never be a child’s suitcase. Every foster child deserves to carry their belongings with dignity — and I need you to help me make that possible,” Kelley wrote in the caption.

The Arlington resident, who holds a master’s degree in public health administration, is also a senior philanthropic adviser for St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital in Arlington, according to her LinkedIn.
With pageant competitions as one of her many hustles, Kelley finds community. She tells TODAY.com what went into her decision to pursue the contests.

“I was a freshman or maybe sophomore in college at the time, just looking for community, looking for like-minded, strong women that wanted to empower and support each other, looking for those types of friendships,” she says. “I found that with pageant women, after doing my first one, I just loved it. I loved the experience and what I got out of it, being in a room full of women that inspire me. That is what keeps me coming back.”

Kelley says her family could not have been more supportive and proud throughout her pageant journey. She says they have been a part of this journey for several years, and that this dream of hers has become their dream.

“My husband keeps calling himself Mr. USA. I don’t know if that’s a thing. Every family member I talk to, they’re like, ‘I can’t believe I’m Miss USA’s aunt. I can’t believe I’m Miss USA’s sister,’ and I’m like, ‘What? Bro, I can’t believe I’m Miss USA.’ This is just  the coolest thing for all of us.”
